items.title: Surge in software patches likely behind recent tech outages, experts say
items.description: Recent disruptions to the way people work, access bank accounts and travel are likely tied to corporate efforts to patch software vulnerabilities in the AI age, experts said.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The JPMorgan Chase building is pictured in New York on Oct. 21, 2025. (Seth Wenig / AP Photo)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Seth Wenig</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Recent disruptions to the way people work, access bank accounts and travel are likely tied to corporate efforts to patch software vulnerabilities in the AI age, experts said.
items.body:
Recent disruptions to the way people work, access bank accounts and travel are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, experts said.

U.S. government officials have sought to reassure the public that the tech outages are not related, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio telling reporters in Manila this week that company patches — software and operating system updates intended to fix security vulnerabilities — are, at times, “creating short-term disruption in the way the system works.”

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also told a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing on worldwide threats Wednesday that there is so far no indication that the tech outages are related.

That said, disruptions to services at JPMorgan Chase on Monday that also affected other banks drew immediate attention from U.S. banking regulators, who have contacted lenders to ensure incidents are contained and not linked to a cyberattack, two people familiar with the matter said.

One of the people said that Treasury officials also were making inquiries.

The advent of easily accessible AI tools and large language models has supercharged the discovery of vulnerabilities in software. Microsoft this month has addressed more than 1,200 software vulnerabilities, nearly 20 times higher than in the same month a year ago, according to cybersecurity firm Qualys.

“AI has made finding critical vulnerabilities fast and cheap, and the number of flaws that demand immediate patching has grown with it,” said Yuval Itzchakov, CTO and co-founder of autonomous offensive security company A Security.

“Emergency patches go into core infrastructure within hours, often without the full testing cycle, and they are intrusive by design: they change runtimes, kernels and network components that everything else depends on. That speed and scale of change is itself a source of failure,” Itzchakov said.

Josh Bressers, director of co-ordinated vulnerability disclosure at cybersecurity firm VulnCheck, said that in 2026 there have been 100,000 publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, tracked by industry as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVEs. Of those, Bressers said, 1,363 were known to have been exploited in the real world.

Bank regulator plans deep dive into issue

Within the banking sector, at least one major bank was rushing to address a wave of recent patches and there is a lot of work needed, a person at the bank said.

After the outage at JPMorgan Chase, lenders received inquiries from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), according to a separate person, who added that the U.S. banking regulator was trying to assess the impact and wanted to know about communication to customers.

The Treasury and the OCC were calling banks minutes after the incident was reported to check that the issue was contained and it was not a cyber-related incident, a third person said.

The banks were asked to communicate to the customers that they should not panic and that everything was under control, that person said.

The OCC is also going to do a deep dive into the issue and check that everything the regulator was told is correct and that there are no other shortcomings, the person added.

All sources spoke on condition of anonymity.

OCC head Jonathan Gould told an industry event on Tuesday that the JPMorgan outage was “an isolated incident.”

“The OCC, as you would expect, was very involved identifying the issue, talking to the bank in question and talking to the other banks that were affected,” he said.

The U.S. Treasury did not respond to a request seeking comment.

Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial, said technology has made banking “incredibly convenient, and while occasional outages can be frustrating, I don’t believe the outages will have a significant impact on consumer confidence or change how most people manage their money.”

“Financial institutions have invested heavily in technology and security, and, unfortunately, occasional disruptions will happen,” Gestiehr said. “What matters most is how quickly those issues are identified, resolved and communicated to customers.”

(Reporting by AJ Vicens in Detroit, Nupur Anand, Stephen Gandal and Saeed Azhar in New York; Editing by Megan Davies, Will Dunham, Diane Craft and Edwina Gibbs)

AJ Vicens and Nupur Anand, Reuters

items.title: Province says new data centre policies will address Albertans’ concern over growing industry
items.description: Alberta is making changes to where some data centres can go.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A person holds a sign that says "No data centres, save our water" during an anti-AI data centre protest at the Alberta legislature in Edmonton on June 27, 2026. (Curtis Goodrum / CTV News Edmonton)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Alberta is making changes to where some data centres can go.
items.body:
Alberta is making changes to where some data centres can go.

The new policies were included in the omnibus Bill 42 tabled on Wednesday encompassing amendments to data centres, oil and gas and the forestry sector.

The province says the Energy, Environment and Utilities Statutes Amendment Act, 2026, responds to Albertans’ concerns over data centres by restricting projects 10 megawatts (MW) or larger from being built within 600 metres of the nearest home or on “high-quality” farmland.

Centres that size would also be prohibited on irrigated land, which the province reports would protect about 14 million acres of Class 1 and 2 agricultural land.

The province said the changes would prevent situations like that in Olds, where a 1.4-gigawatt (GW) facility was announced on the east side of the town. The proposal sparked public backlash and was eventually rejected.

“This will give communities like Olds that confidence that this can never happen in their backyard, and they don’t have to wait for months and months and months for a regulatory process to unfold,” Technology Minster Nate Glubish said.

Glubish said feedback from Albertans informed the new policies.

To address environmental concerns, the Alberta Utilities Commission (AUC) would become the regulator of all centres 10 WM or larger, which Glubish said would ensure projects are held to the same noise and light standards as power plants.

He added the bill would also support the development of regulations that would define efficiency standards for water use.

Jorden Dye, director of the Business Renewable Centre of Canada, said water limitations are good news, but added the bill is lacking regarding other environmental concerns.

For example, centres connecting to the grid will have to be gas-powered.

  • Why renewables are being left out of Alberta’s data centre power plans

“We have a significant increase in emissions coming if the currently proposed data centres are built out,” Dye said. “It would be about 1.8 times the emissions of Canada’s entire energy grid.”

“I would also raise that the Alberta government is currently reviewing renewable setbacks and is proposing to allow municipalities to restrict those to up to 1,500 metres,” he added.

“if that goes forward, we could see a world next year where a data centre could be half as close to your your house as a solar farm.”

Affordability

The province says the new legislation would address affordability worries over data centre development by addressing high distribution costs in some areas and requiring centres pay for any infrastructure needed to access the grid.

“Down the road, there is and can be a great benefit when you have large-load users like this that can pick up the majority of the transmission costs,” Minister of Affordability and Utilities RJ Sigurdson, said.

Dye said nothing in the new bill would protect Albertans from rising energy prices caused by centres’ increased demand on the grid.

For example, the hyperscale 1-GW Meta facility in Sturgeon County has been approved to pull 970 MW from the grid when it comes online years before its own power source is ready.

“The actual concern for Albertans, their power bills, will go up during the bridging period,” Dye said.

A report from the Pembina Institute this year estimated that connection could add hundreds of dollars to Albertan’s annual energy bills and offset the benefits of lower transmission fees.

The Alberta Electric System Operator (AESO) said in August that wholesale electricity prices were expected to increase due to more demand, but added that demand would in turn “attract new supply” that would later lower prices.

  • Meta data centre could drive up Albertans’ power bills: report

“This is how the market balances prices over time and signals when and where supply is needed,” the AESO said.

Neither Sigurdson nor Glubish directly answered questions when asked about rising electricity prices on Wednesday.

“We’re taking a look at what’s necessary to make sure we have the merchant power available, the buildouts happening in the province, to make sure that we continue to have the most affordable utilities in Canada,” Sigurdson said on Wednesday.

The province reports that there are 70 data centres currently working with its concierge program and that 30 per cent of those could be impacted by the new policies.

Projects with already approved permits will not be subject to the new policies, Glubish said.

He said, if Bill 42 passes, the AUC will be responsible for public engagement on data centres and Albertans with concerns can file a complaint with that regulator.

Changes in the bill regarding other industries include:

  • increased penalties for illegal dumping and other environmental contamination;
  • the creation of a new fund for oil and gas cleanup and reclamation;
  • increasing market access to forests; and
  • repealing the Oil Sands Emissions Limit Act, which the province said was never implemented.

items.title: Anthropic clinches biggest IPO ever with US$81 billion offering
items.description: Anthropic’s IPO raised US$81.31 billion on Wednesday, eclipsing SpaceX’s offering to claim the title of the largest stock-market debut on record.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[SpaceX employees celebrate during a closing bell ceremony for the IPO of SpaceX at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, Friday, June 12, 2026, in New York. items._ogDesc: Anthropic’s IPO raised US$81.31 billion on Wednesday, eclipsing SpaceX’s offering to claim the title of the largest stock-market debut on record.
items.body:
Anthropic’s IPO raised US$81.31 billion on Wednesday, eclipsing SpaceX’s offering to claim the title of the largest stock-market debut on record.

Anthropic said the IPO was priced at US$83 apiece, above its previously targeted range and valuing the company at approximately US$1.5 trillion.

Reuters was first to report earlier that IPO was upsized by about 19 per cent to 980 million shares from its initial plan to sell 825 million shares at between US$70 and US$78 apiece. Anthropic is also raising US$26 billion through a private placement at the IPO price, the filings show.

On a fully diluted basis, the IPO values the company at about US$1.5 trillion including securities such as stock options and restricted stock. On a non-diluted basis, the valuation stands at about US$1.1 trillion.

Anthropic, the first major frontier artificial-intelligence model developer to do an IPO, follows SpaceX’s SPCX.O June offering, as investors jump at the chance for exposure to the fast-growing industry, even as the industry also faces mounting questions over the cost of developing and operating artificial intelligence models.

Latest updates on company news here

Challenging backdrop for AI stocks

The AI lab comes to the public market just months after SpaceX’s record-setting IPO, even as the backdrop for AI stocks has turned more challenging. Chipmakers and cloud companies central to the business have come under pressure in recent weeks due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs and the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of chipmaker Nvidia NVDA.O, a key pillar of the industry’s growth.

The pricing follows a roadshow that attracted demand several times the number of shares offered, Reuters previously reported, despite questions about the company’s outlook and its ability to sustain rapid growth as competition in the AI industry intensifies.

The company’s closest rival, OpenAI, is also expected to pursue a public listing as early as next year.

Anthropic’s growth has been driven by surging demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code, its coding agent that has gained popularity among software developers. Its annualized revenue run rate reached US$81 billion as of Oct. 31, up US$10 billion from Sept. 30, according to its IPO filing.

The Claude maker said it had 11,900 customers generating at least US$100,000 in annual revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as of Sept. 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of last year, underscoring its growing business foothold.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

Spending commitments expose risks

But sustaining that growth is becoming expensive. Anthropic spent nearly US$9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the amount spent a year earlier. It also incurred an additional US$5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter, weighing on efficiency and reducing the revenue generated per dollar of computing capacity.

Revenue rose 47 per cent in the third quarter to US$16.96 billion from the second quarter. The company reported an operating loss of $567 million, compared with operating income of US$974 million in the previous quarter. The net loss narrowed to US$23.3 billion from $66.3 billion a quarter earlier, including non-operating ​items related to bonds convertible into its shares.

Anthropic has committed to nearly US$900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon AMZN.O and Alphabet’s GOOGL.O Google, part of its ongoing expenditures to train and operate increasingly powerful AI models.

Its spending commitments also expose the company to risks beyond its own finances. Anthropic warned in its prospectus that some of its computing providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing and credit support to acquire chips and build capacity.

“If such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered,” Anthropic said in an IPO filing.

Investors have grown increasingly concerned about debt-fueled expansion of AI infrastructure, with technology companies and data-center operators borrowing heavily to finance chips, power and computing facilities.

Anthropic also faces questions over how it will balance its commercial ambitions with its emphasis on AI safety. CEO Dario Amodei has called for the industry to slow the pace of developing and releasing increasingly powerful models, warning that advances in AI could outstrip society’s ability to manage the risks.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Competition and safety challenges

Competition is intensifying against Anthropic to be the leading provider of AI tools for businesses.

OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, its latest flagship AI model, accounted for about 13 per cent of enterprise AI spending tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with about eight per cent for Anthropic’s Claude Fable, according to data cited by Reuters in September. OpenAI’s annualized revenue run rate also passed US$40 billion in July, although Anthropic maintained a lead at the time.

The competitive threat extends beyond the handful of companies developing the most powerful commercial models. More large companies are looking to adopt these models, which can be downloaded and run independently, to rein in AI spending.

A recent Capgemini study found that 59 per cent of executives at large companies plan to increase their use of open-weight models over the next year as AI costs exceed budgets.

Meta Platforms, one of Anthropic’s largest customers, has been looking to reduce its use of the startup’s models as it develops more AI capabilities internally, Reuters previously reported.

“There’s going to be other models out there ... Our thesis is that the vast amount of value will accrue to whoever is at the frontier,” said Peter Singlehurst, head of private companies at Baillie Gifford, which invested roughly US$1.5 billion in Anthropic before its IPO. “Our bet is that Anthropic has the ingredients — that doesn’t guarantee, but means that they arguably have the highest probability of remaining at the frontier.”

Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warned that its models could develop capabilities faster than the company could evaluate them and put adequate safeguards in place.

“Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm,” Anthropic said in the filing.

The company has said it is considering tighter human oversight of some research and development decisions as its AI models take on a growing share of that work.

Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters for Anthropic’s offering, which has a 22-bank underwriting syndicate. The two banks also served as lead underwriters for SpaceX’s IPO earlier this year.

(Reporting by Echo Wang in New York; Editing by David Gaffen, Christian Plumb, Matthew Lewis and Sonali Paul)

items.title: Trump meets Xi and Putin in China with nuclear arms and two wars on the table
items.description: U.S. President Donald Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to their already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a U.S. official confirmed.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[China's President Xi Jinping stands as U.S. President Donald Trump, left, and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, Wednesday Nov.Â 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via AP)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Iori Sagisawa</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to their already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a U.S. official confirmed.
items.body:
SHENZHEN, China -- When U.S. President Donald Trump meets Thursday with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, it could mark a pivot in world history -- or become a quickly forgotten photo op.

Trump, who will test his reputation as an expert dealmaker in the trilateral meeting, has promoted his time with Xi and Putin -- two of America’s leading rivals -- as a chance to hash out rules for controlling nuclear arms and to start resolving the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Experts have kept expectations low for major breakthroughs.

The president said the advantage of meeting the two autocrats at the same time would be because their countries work together.

“They both like Trump. Now, what happens after me? That I can’t tell you,” Trump said in a Thursday interview with Fox News.

Trump plans to have a separate one-on-one meeting with Xi -- his third substantial meeting with him this year -- right before the trilateral. He also added a separate sit-down with Putin to his schedule, marking the first time the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, even as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.

Along for the trip -- but so far keeping a low profile -- is Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX has intermittently throttled the military-grade Starshield satellite system used by Ukraine for launching its drones and intercepting hits from Russia.

One meeting is unlikely to produce a breakthrough in nuclear talks

The trilateral is scheduled to occur after a session with leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit on Thursday morning and is expected to be the capstone to Trump’s Asia trip that started Tuesday in the Philippines.

Trump has said he wants to talk to the leaders about their nuclear stockpiles. The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.

Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said Trump’s showmanship could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.

“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump at APEC,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”

Trump told Fox News in his interview that “it’s a very hard thing to do” to ask a leader to reduce nuclear stockpiles.

Trump boasts about his relationships. But the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger

Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters that Putin, Trump and Xi would likely touch on the war in Ukraine, though the agenda was not fully set. Trump has said he wants to discuss that war -- as well as the conflict in Iran.

His ambitions recall an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump is negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine -- or countries like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.

The U.S. president has openly pursued a Nobel Peace Prize even as he took military action against Venezuela and Iran. He also threatened earlier this year to take Greenland by force from Denmark, a gambit that led to an agreement for the construction of U.S. military bases.

Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi appealed to his ego Wednesday by greeting Air Force One on the airport tarmac, as the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.

But Trump does not appear to always have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share. For all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, the warmth has not always been mutually effusive.

On Wednesday at APEC, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions.

“China-Russia relations have remained steadfast through storms while taking a long-term view,” Xi said to Putin. “They have brought greater stability and certainty to a world marked by intertwined changes and turbulence.”

The pair discussed the war in Ukraine during their talks, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.

By contrast, when Xi came to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a “personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi plan to meet a total of four times this year, with their final time together coming in December at the G20 summit being held at the Trump National Doral Golf Club in Florida.

Ukraine and its European allies are suspicious of the trilateral meeting that could potentially cut them out of the process. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said Europeans feared another “Anchorage moment,” a reference to last year’s Putin-Trump meeting in Alaska that produced proposals that were rejected by Ukraine and its partners.

Conflicts on AI and trade also hang over the meetings

While Trump views his relationship with China as a positive, it has not necessarily resulted in meaningful changes between the world’s two largest economies. China continues to run large trade surpluses with the rest of the world, while the U.S. has almost equally large trade deficits.

And the race between the U.S. and China to master artificial intelligence has grown tense over the past two weeks. Trump ally Jensen Huang resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia after confessing to an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whose company helped to give China access to the company’s advanced computer chips used to develop AI models. Beijing has denied that Alice Huang was a Chinese government agent.

Trump held off on imposing tougher restrictions on China’s ability to access the chips, suggesting he did not want to insult China and aggravate relations.

Before APEC, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.

The U.S. officials said afterward that China had not fully honored its commitments made last year in a Trump-Xi meeting to buy more U.S. agricultural products and loosen restrictions on the sale of rare earth minerals needed for electronics.

The trade truce between the U.S. and China reached last year after dueling tariff hikes is set to expire by Jan. 10 next year.

Trump officials have dangled the possibility of opening up highly sanctioned trade with Russia as an incentive for ending hostilities in Ukraine, and Trump has frequently demonstrated that he sees trade as a foreign policy tool.

Meanwhile, both China and Russia have used trade to support Iran, even during the U.S. war on that country, which has pushed up energy prices and reduced global economic growth.

Josh Boak and Michelle L. Price, The Associated Press

Price reported from Manila, Philippines. AP writers Darlene Superville in Washington and Jim Gomez in Manila contributed to this report

Associated Press writer Will Weissert in Washington contributed to this report.

items.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ is almost here. What to know about the characters, music and all the hype
items.description: After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A billboard announcing the release of the "Grand Theft Auto VI" video game is displayed near Times Square, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Yuki Iwamura</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here.
items.body:
LOS ANGELES — “Grand Theft Auto” has never been much for following the rules.

Nearly three decades after a video game built around stealing cars, outrunning police and embracing criminal mayhem first arrived, the franchise has survived controversy, transformed open-world gaming and become one of the biggest sellers in entertainment.

Now, after a 13-year wait since its last main installment, “Grand Theft Auto VI” is preparing for another big score. The latest chapter arrives Thursday with a return to the neon-soaked streets of Vice City with two protagonists.

For longtime fans, “GTA VI” is a highly anticipated return. For everyone else, here’s what to know about the blockbuster video game, its characters and the enormous business riding on its release.

The game also picked up eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, best game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.

Why is ‘Grand Theft Auto’ such a big deal?

The franchise began in 1997 as a relatively simple, top-down game that allowed players to roam fictional cities, steal vehicles, evade police and commit crimes.

The release of “Grand Theft Auto III” in 2001 helped redefine open-world gaming. It gave players greater freedom to explore a sprawling three-dimensional city, pursue missions and interact with their surroundings.

Later installments expanded that freedom with larger environments, cinematic storytelling, social satire and detailed worlds. The influence reached far beyond games about stealing cars.

Ubisoft’s Assassin’s Creed series brought open-world exploration to historical settings, while Bethesda’s The Elder Scrolls games expanded their own longstanding tradition of open-ended fantasy role-playing. Nintendo’s “The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild” later emphasized experimentation and discovery, allowing players to use the environment itself to solve problems.

For “Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas” and “Grand Theft Auto V,” Rockstar Games recruited real-life gang members to help bring authenticity to background characters and dialogue. Former writer and audio director Lazlow Jones has said some performers challenged scripted lines, prompting developers to let them use language drawn from their own experiences.

That attention to detail helped create the sense of a living world that became a hallmark of the franchise, even as the series drew criticism for its depictions of violence, crime and women.

But controversy did not stop the franchise’s commercial rise.

According to publisher Take-Two Interactive, the franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those units and reached US$1 billion in retail sales in just three days.

Its online multiplayer component, “Grand Theft Auto Online,” has helped keep players engaged through years of updates, new activities and in-game purchases.

When can players start playing ‘GTA VI’?

“Grand Theft Auto VI” will become playable at midnight local time on Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X’S, according to Rockstar Games.

That means players can begin playing at 12 a.m. in their respective time zones. In the United States, the game unlocks at midnight Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific time as that day begins in each region.

Players who preordered the game digitally can already preload it, allowing the game files to be downloaded before launch. Preloading does not provide early access.

How closely is Vice City based on Miami?

“Grand Theft Auto VI” returns players to Vice City, Rockstar Games’ fictional version of Miami and South Florida. Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture. Rockstar has promised its largest and most detailed open-world experience yet.

Miami is also leaning into its fictional alter ego ahead of the release. Miami-Dade County struck a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center, while Miami and Miami Beach have launched their own promotions tied to the game. The Heat will also wear black-and-pink “Vice City” jerseys on the eve of the release.

Not everyone has embraced the connection. Some South Florida officials have criticized using public resources to promote a franchise known for crime and violence, while supporters argue the campaign allows the region to capitalize on the enormous attention surrounding the game.

What’s the story behind ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’?

This time, the action returns to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, and expands across the surrounding state of Leonida, a Florida-inspired setting filled with beaches, highways, nightlife and criminal enterprises.

At the centre are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple trying to improve their circumstances through a life of crime. Lucia has recently been released from prison while Jason, a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys, is looking for a different path.

Their plans become more complicated when a seemingly straightforward criminal job goes wrong, drawing them into a conspiracy that stretches across Leonida.

The trailers suggest a story mixing romance, robberies, betrayals and the series’ familiar satirical take on American culture.

Rockstar has revealed several supporting characters, including bank robber Raul Bautista, aspiring music executive Dre’Quan Priest and nightclub owner Boobie Ike.

Who’s in the cast?

Rockstar has kept much of the voice cast under wraps, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason.

One familiar actor has confirmed his involvement: Stephen Root, known for his work in “Office Space,” “King of the Hill” and “Barry.” He told The Associated Press in September that he appears in the game, adding that fans had already recognized his distinctive voice in promotional footage.

Root has been identified in reports as the voice of Brian Heder, an aging drug runner operating out of the Leonida Keys. Rockstar has introduced the character but has not publicly confirmed Root’s casting in that specific role.

What makes this installment different?

Beyond the return to Vice City, one of the biggest changes is the focus on two protagonists whose relationship drives the story.

“Grand Theft Auto V” featured three playable main characters. The new installment centres on Lucia and Jason as partners navigating the criminal underworld together.

Rockstar has promoted a larger, more detailed setting that stretches beyond the city into the wider state of Leonida. The game also arrives in a vastly different technological landscape from its predecessor, with newer consoles capable of supporting more elaborate environments and character interactions.

But not every detail is known. Rockstar has offered trailers and promotional previews, while questions remain about the full range of activities, how the game’s systems will work and the future of its online multiplayer experience.

What about the music?

Music has long been part of Grand Theft Auto’s identity. It has included everything from fictional radio stations to the songs accompanying players as they cruise through the game’s cities.

“Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album,” a 34-track collection of original songs tied to the game, is scheduled for release Friday.

A separate 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” by Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo of Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay, is scheduled for Dec. 11.

Rockstar says the score adapts to players’ actions and experiences throughout the game, shifting with the environments and situations they encounter. It features collaborations with artists including Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.

The game also features in-game radio stations, continuing the franchise’s long connection to popular music.

Jonathan Landrum Jr., The Associated Press

Associated Press journalists Charlotte Graham-McLay in Wellington, New Zealand, and Tong-hyung Kim in Seoul contributed to this report.

items._ogDesc: Norwegian Cruise Line is setting sail in a different direction, scrapping nearly 20 stops in Halifax, N.S., next year to spend more time in Bermuda instead.
items.body:
Norwegian Cruise Line is setting sail in a different direction, scrapping nearly 20 stops in Halifax, N.S., next year to spend more time in Bermuda instead.

Its Breakaway ship typically travels from Boston to Halifax before heading south. But in an email to guests and travel partners, the cruise line says it has “enhanced” its itinerary — meaning some trips will opt for an “extended stay” in Royal Naval Dockyard, Bermuda.

The change, which will see the cruise line drop 17 stops in Halifax in 2027, comes “in response to guest feedback,” according to the email from Norwegian.

The “original” itinerary saw the Breakaway dock in Halifax for less than a day, from 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Now, travellers will spend that day at sea before arriving in Bermuda a day early — giving them two nights on the tropical island.

The email to guests, which was shared in the Norwegian Breakaway 2026 and 2027 Boston to Bermuda Facebook group, included the “revised” itinerary.

“By spending two nights on the island, you’ll have even more time to discover Bermuda at your own pace, enjoy its unique culture and natural beauty, and experience the destination both during the day and after sunset,” it reads.

Norwegian Cruise Line called the revision an “enhancement,” adding that “Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada will no longer be included in your itinerary.”

‘Very disappointed’

Online users gave mixed reactions to the change.

In the Facebook group, one person commented that they were “excited for the original itinerary because we haven’t been to either Nova Scotia or Bermuda,” adding, “we are considering cancelling because of the change.”

“Us too!” another person said. “Very disappointed.”

‘It was really cold’

On the other hand, one person who previously travelled to Halifax said, “it felt like the area wasn’t super excited about having a cruise arrive.

“Lots of neat looking shops and a brewery, but (they) were closed.”

Another who did the cruise last year said they found Nova Scotia “lovely” but shared that their “main complaint was that it was really cold … heading north.”

Another commenter added, “It’s not (that) the people don’t like Nova Scotia. But you’re going on a cruise to Bermuda, people want to spend time in Bermuda…”

But Norwegian Cruise Line isn’t saying goodbye to Halifax.

A company spokesperson told CTV News on Wednesday that while the city is “no longer featured on specific voyages,” guests will still be able to visit the city on its Canada and New England itineraries throughout 2027 and 2028.

Halifax wraps up a ‘strong season’

At the start of the 2026 cruise ship season, Port Halifax anticipated 189 calls by 28 cruise lines, bringing approximately 363,000 guests. Officials described it as a “strong season” with “new itineraries and new homeports calling Halifax and the region.”

A 2026 highlight for the port authority was Norwegian Cruise Line’s “increased presence in spring and summer with the addition of Bermuda itineraries that include a stop in Halifax.”

  • READ MORE: Four cruise-ships in one day: what is behind one of Halifax’s biggest cruise seasons yet?

The outgoing season wrapped up on Nov. 5.

Port Halifax also pointed to a 2023 study by the Cruise Lines International Association, which found that cruise generates nearly $200 million each year and close to 1,000 jobs in Nova Scotia, supporting businesses and attractions.

An unexpected cruise ship visit came to Halifax in October, when The Oasis of the Seas departed New Jersey with thousands of passengers who paid to go to the Bahamas — only to have stormy weather divert them to Nova Scotia’s capital instead.

‘Halifax is a beautiful city’

Some travellers felt hopeful, while others lost their enthusiasm.

“I am already from Canada, and I wanted to go to the Bahamas,” Toronto’s Nicholas Meli told CTV News last month. “I’m very disappointed.”

Meanwhile, Walter MacDonnell of Hamilton, Ont., said: “I’m glad this happened because we are loving it here. I was really impressed when I came here before.”

“Halifax is a beautiful city,” added New Jersey’s Jim Matthews.

Port Halifax lauds the city as a “world-class destination” that continues to see solid cruise growth year-over-year, remaining “the marquee cruise destination in Atlantic Canada with the ability to accommodate the world’s largest cruise ships.”

With files from CTV News’ Paul Hollingsworth, The Canadian Press

items.description: The Competition Bureau says it has obtained a court order to advance an ongoing investigation into Old Navy and Gap.

items._ogDesc: The Competition Bureau says it has obtained a court order to advance an ongoing investigation into Old Navy and Gap.
items.body:
The Competition Bureau says it has obtained a court order to advance an ongoing investigation into Old Navy and Gap.

The independent law enforcement agency said on Wednesday that the investigation involves “potentially false or misleading claims” made by the clothing brands, each operated by Gap Inc.

“The Bureau is seeking to determine whether specific marketing practices used by Old Navy and Gap raise concerns under the deceptive marketing provisions of the Competition Act. There has been no finding of wrongdoing at this time,” the Competition Bureau said in a news release.

The agency says its investigation will examine whether regular prices are genuine when products are advertised as being “on sale,” as well as urgency cues such as limited-time offers and countdown timers.

The investigation will also examine promotional messages such as “Selling Fast” or “Only a Few Left,” which suggest products are in short supply.

According to the news release, Old Navy and Gap will be required to produce records and written information relevant to the Bureau’s investigation.

A Gap Inc. spokesperson told CTV News on Wednesday that the company is co-operating with the Competition Bureau’s inquiry.

“We take our responsibility to provide customers with clear and accurate information seriously,” the spokesperson wrote.

“As the Bureau itself has acknowledged, no findings of wrongdoing have been made.”

Given the ongoing investigation, Gap Inc. said it will make no further comments.

News about the investigation comes just a week ahead of Black Friday, on Nov. 27, when brands frequently advertise price drops and their largest annual discounts.

The agency says it is committed to protecting “consumers from deceptive marketing practices in the digital economy,” and says it saw an increase in complaints about “inflated regular prices” in 2025.

In the same year, the agency published a warning to businesses reminding them that it’s illegal to advertise fake discounts by promoting a made-up “regular price.”

items.body:
NEW YORK — Skydance will combine two of its key TV production units, Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios, bringing such shows as “The Pitt,” “Ted Lasso,” “Reacher” and “Landman” under the same roof.

The combined entity will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios, with Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell serving as presidents. The merger of the studios will be completed in early 2027, according to a memo released Wednesday.

“Bringing together two of the industry’s most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine, uniting extraordinary talent, resources, acclaimed programming and iconic franchises with the global scale to compete at the highest level,” George Cheeks, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV, said in the memo.

It’s the latest move since Skydance-owned Paramount last month closed its US$81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, ushering in a new Hollywood giant under the leadership of David Ellison.

The new Warner Bros. Television Studios will house more than 120 TV series, including HBO’s “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone,” Netflix’s “Emily in Paris” and CBS’ “Marshals.”

CBS Studios — another studio that produces shows such as the “NCIS” and “Fire Country” franchises — will continue to operate as a standalone entity under David Stapf.

items.description: A fifth straight drop for the S&P 500 dragged Wall Street to its longest losing streak since June, as Nvidia and other tech stocks kept swinging on uncertainty.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Traders Fred Demarco, left, and Edward McCarthy work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Monday, Nov. 24, 2025. (AP Photo/Richard Drew)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Richard Drew</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A fifth straight drop for the S&P 500 dragged Wall Street to its longest losing streak since June, as Nvidia and other tech stocks kept swinging on uncertainty.
items.body:
NEW YORK — A fifth straight drop for the S&P 500 on Wednesday dragged Wall Street to its longest losing streak since June, as Nvidia and other stocks tied to artificial intelligence technology kept swinging on uncertainty about how much strength is left in the AI boom.

The S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent after zigzagging between gains and losses through the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 561 points, or 1.1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite added 0.4 per cent.

Nvidia once again was at the centre of the market’s moves. Its stock initially jumped 2.7 per cent after the chip company reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Perhaps more importantly, it also gave a forecast for revenue in the current quarter that was better than expected.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

But the stock quickly erased all its gain and then finished with a loss of 2.9 per cent.

The question is whether Nvidia’s big growth can continue despite the turmoil created by the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. He had an immense personality that drew attention and investment to AI, and he built Nvidia into a company so big that it helped to fund some of the industry’s growth itself.

“Our momentum is real,” Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, told investors and financial analysts after announcing the company’s latest results. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We’ve got this.”

The encouraging numbers and words coming from Nvidia, though, failed to create lasting gains for the price of its stock or for others across the industry.

Micron Technology, whose sales of memory chips exploded with the AI boom, went from an early rise of 1.5 per cent to a drop of 1 per cent.

CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents access to them out to customers over the cloud, sank 4.1 per cent and has lost nearly a third of its value so far this year.

The entire industry has been swinging recently. Besides criticism that AI stock prices simply shot too high in their frenzy, the industry is facing worries that this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections could mean more regulation for it.

Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks of oil companies were heavy weights due to drops for oil prices. ExxonMobil fell four per cent, and Chevron sank 4 per cent after the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.3 per cent to settle at US$91.95.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

The drop in oil prices helped to pull yields down in the bond market, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 5.06 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Tuesday.

High yields have made mortgages more expensive to get, which has chilled the housing industry. But they’ve moderated over the last month, and a report on Wednesday said homebuilders broke ground on more projects last month than economists expected.

That helped push stocks of homebuilders modestly higher, and Lennar added 0.7 per cent.

Some of the strongest gains on Wall Street came from retailers following their profit reports.

TJX rallied 8 per cent after the company behind the TJ Maxx and Marshalls stores reported slightly better earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Ernie Herrman said he expects momentum to accelerate through the holiday shopping season.

Target climbed four per cent following a better-than-expected profit report, which included its strongest quarterly sales gain in roughly five years.

Take-Two Interactive Software revved 6.2 per cent higher amid glowing reviews for its latest “Grand Theft Auto” video game.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 16.90 points to 7,323.63. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 561.25 to 50,198.17, and the Nasdaq composite rose 101.50 to 24,429.88.

In stock markets abroad, indexes fell in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia.

  • Latest updates on investing here

London’s FTSE 100 sank 1.3 per cent after a report said inflation in the United Kingdom worsened. That could up the pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates to get inflation under control.

Expectations are high that the Federal Reserve in Washington will raise its own interest rate when it meets next month, after it made no move last month. Notes released Wednesday from the Fed’s latest meeting indicated some officials are considering a larger increase to rates than usual in December.

South Korea’s Kospi jumped 2 per cent a day after dropping to its lowest closing level since February. It’s swung in particular because its market is dominated by two stocks tied to the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report.

items.description: Ontario officials said Wednesday they’re hopeful that a meeting with the global CEO of automaker Stellantis will have a good result for the fate of some 2,200 employees who could be without jobs if a planned sale of the company’s Brampton plant goes ahead.

items._ogDesc: Ontario officials said Wednesday they’re hopeful that a meeting with the global CEO of automaker Stellantis will have a good result for the fate of some 2,200 employees who could be without jobs if a planned sale of the company’s Brampton plant goes ahead.
items.body:
Ontario officials said Wednesday they’re hopeful that a meeting with the global CEO of automaker Stellantis will have a good result for the fate of some 2,200 employees who could be without jobs if a planned sale of the company’s Brampton plant goes ahead.

Speaking with reporters at Queen’s Park, Premier Doug Ford said he’ll be at a meeting with Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa and federal Industry Minister Melanie Joly Friday.

“We’re going to meet with (him) and see where they stand,” Ford said. “Our goal is always to make sure that we bring back the jobs to the Brampton facility.”

Ford said the plant had been losing $150 million a year and suggested that could be resolved by easing a federal regulatory burden that costs roughly twice that much.

“If we want to be competitive, we have to get rid of the regulatory burden that the federal government has on them,” Ford said.

Ontario Industry Minister Vic Fedeli also spoke with reporters and expressed optimism about the meeting.

“Let’s see what happens on Friday. We’re hopeful and confident that we have a good meeting on Friday,” Fedeli said.

Asked if the Stellantis should have to pay back more than the $24 million of federal grant money they have said they will repay if the plant does close, Fedeli said the province has not handed the company anything for the Brampton facility to date.

“All I would say is the province of Ontario has not given them any money, so it’s not right to say we’re giving them more money. We haven’t given them anything yet,” Fedeli said.

There is a $2.5 billion joint federal-provincial fund meant to bolster the auto industry, though its unclear if Stellantis could be provided incentives with that funding in exchange for keeping the plant open.

Joly has said that the federal government is tabling an “aggressive package” aimed at getting the company to stay. However she has warned that if they proceed to sell of the Brampton plant to defence contractor Roshel, they would be on the hook to repay hundreds of millions of dollars in federal money they received.

Joly has said she is willing to sue Stellantis to recover the money if need be.

She reiterated that point Friday and said she will be speaking with Ontario and union officials as well.

“When it comes to dealing with Stellantis, we will be meeting with the Government of Ontario because they have to play their part.” Joly told reporters. “We will work also with the union because we need to make sure also that they do their part and we will meet with Stellantis because they also need to do their part.”

The company closed the plant in 2023 to retool it so that it could switch from making Chrysler vehicles to electric Jeep vehicles, but they paused their retooling plan, leaving the workers in limbo. Stellantis announced earlier this month they intend to sell the plant to Roshel, which has said it would not carry over any promises Stellantis previously made to workers at the plant.

In a statement provided to CTV News on Wednesday, a spokesperson said that Stellantis “remains committed to engaging constructively with the Canadian and Ontario governments and Unifor regarding the sale of Brampton Assembly Plant.”

“Our priority remains on working constructively with Unifor toward a fair, negotiated resolution that supports affected employees and recognizes their years of service,” the statement notes.

items.title: Start with the problem, not the tech: how brokers should adopt AI
items.description: Fintech consultancy founder on the steps brokers need to take
items.content: <p>Fintech consultancy founder on the steps brokers need to take</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_639306290579590103.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Fintech consultancy founder on the steps brokers need to take
items.body:
Artificial intelligence is a hot topic for mortgage brokers – but should they adopt technology for its own sake? Alfred Yang, founder of fintech consultancy Finnovate.io, told CMP about the steps brokers should be taking to bring AI into their brokerage.

[00:00] Aldred Young: Certainly, brokers are not going to be replaced by AI. As a homeowner myself, right? I prefer to talk to a human being and get, you know, sound advice.

[00:18] Fergal McAlinden: All right. Well, next up in our day two series of interviews at Markets Fest, we're joined by Aldred Young, who is the founder of Fin Innovate. Aldred, great to have you at the event. So, what are the main messages that you're bringing to brokers and members of the industry about the service that Fin Innovate is providing?

[00:34] Aldred Young: Yeah. So, fininnovate.io, we're a FinTech consultancy. So, we help mortgage brokers and also lenders implement technology to help them accelerate business outcomes. So, everything from back office automation to enhancing their client experiences. So, at the end of the day, I think my message would be to think about how technology can address certain challenges in their business as opposed to just applying technology for the sake of applying technology. So, start with the problems they're seeing in their business and applying the right technologies to address those problems. So, the main message is really just start with the problem and go from there.

[01:18] Fergal McAlinden: It's really interesting. We've been talking about the rise of artificial intelligence in the industry over the past couple of years. I know that it's not necessarily a blanket solution for everything that brokers and other industry members have. That's getting your message as well, that tech is worth it.

[01:33] Aldred Young: Yeah. So, again, right? Start by identifying a business problem that could be a quick win for you if addressed by technology. AI is certainly interesting. It's certainly a hot topic at this conference today. I would say that there's a lot of potential. Like we've heard about automation with AI, summarizing documents with AI, helping with underwriting and lending decisions with AI. I mean, all those fairly salient use cases.

[02:02] We've seen in the industry rapid experimentation with AI. So, for example, any organization that runs ads knows that they need to constantly be tweaking and iterating on messages to consumers and to businesses. So AI could really accelerate the prototyping and the tweaking of the message that you're conveying to your clients. So, we're working with a few organizations today to adopt AI to do these type of rapid prototyping and AB tests to fine tune the message that they're conveying to the market, which in turn helps them accelerate business outcomes.

[02:45] Fergal McAlinden: What would you say to brokers or other industry members who maybe are a little bit skeptical about AI or not sure about using it in their business? We heard on a panel yesterday there were some, I guess, some doubts about AI in the industry. What do you think about that?

[02:58] Aldred Young: Yeah, I would say start small, right? I think AI is a very powerful tool, but at the same time comes risks when you're exposing your data to these large language models. So I think it's important to find the bottlenecks in your business processes, find the bottlenecks in your customer acquisition funnel, and identify one part of it that could potentially be addressed with AI and start there, right?

[03:28] Maybe start with data that is not so sensitive about your clients and start with data that is unique to your organization, but at the same time non-sensitive to your clients. Start there, start small, test it out and get some quick wins.

[03:46] Fergal McAlinden: Are there any trends that maybe aren't as prominent at the moment, but you think will be a big factor in the mortgage space in the next months and years ahead?

[03:54] Aldred Young: Yeah, I would say there's opportunity in both the back office automation, like with KYC, with fraud detection, with automating underwriting decisions. I think there's huge opportunity in the back office, but at the same time on the customer acquisition side, like I said before, there's immense opportunity for you to automate and test your messages to the market using AI, just rapidly prototyping with human feedback in the loop.

[04:28] Fergal McAlinden: I heard a good line yesterday on one of the panels that brokers won't be replaced by AI, but brokers that don't use it might be replaced by brokers that do use it. So the importance of adopting it is really paramount.

[04:40] Aldred Young: Yeah, I would say certainly brokers are not going to be replaced by AI because, as a homeowner myself, right, I'd prefer to talk to a human being and get sound advice, but I think AI can take a lot of the mundane work out of a broker's preparation before speaking to a client. All the document collection, all the boring tasks. Basically, automation allows brokers to free up much of their time and spend more time with their clients.

[05:14] Like AI can certainly help and elevate the client experience, but it certainly wouldn't replace the broker.

[05:21] Fergal McAlinden: That's great. Well, any last message that you'd like to share or anything else that you're excited to announce you're working on?

[05:27] Aldred Young: Yeah, I would say we're excited about the prospect of the rapid advancement in technology and see how it would accelerate businesses not just in lending, but in wealth management, in financial services in general. And we're happy to be a part of it and we love to talk to anyone who feels like technology could help their business and we'd love to have a conversation.

[05:54] Fergal McAlinden: Great stuff. Okay, well, great to talk to you today. Enjoy the rest of the show and we'll talk to you soon.

[05:58] Aldred Young: Yeah, thank you so much.

items.title: Housing minister won't reaffirm Liberal pledge to double home construction
items.description: OTTAWA — Housing Minister Gregor Robertson wouldn't reaffirm the Liberal government's long-standing goal of doubling the pace of home building when pressed by reporters on Wednesday.
items._ogDesc: OTTAWA — Housing Minister Gregor Robertson wouldn't reaffirm the Liberal government's long-standing goal of doubling the pace of home building when pressed by reporters on Wednesday.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Housing Minister Gregor Robertson wouldn't reaffirm the Liberal government's long-standing goal of doubling the pace of home building when pressed by reporters on Wednesday.

The Liberals campaigned during the 2025 election on a pledge to double the annual pace of housing starts to roughly 500,000 over a decade.

But that promise was absent from the federal budget tabled on Nov. 5. The Liberal government instead set new goals in Budget 2026 to triple the pace of non-market housing construction over the next decade and to end homelessness.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan noted the missing reference to doubling home construction in a series of reports analyzing the budget published Tuesday.

"While Budget 2026 announces new measures for homelessness and housing affordability, it is not on track to double housing starts per Budget 2025, with year-to-date housing starts 4 per cent lower in 2026 than 2025," one of Ryan's report read.

The Canadian Press asked Robertson's office last week whether the Liberals were sticking to the target. A spokesperson for his office pointed to a statement sent to The Canadian Press six months earlier reaffirming the pledge.

Reporters asked Robertson as he was heading into the Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday if the government is sticking to the pledge it campaigned on a year and a half ago.

"We're just focused on supply overall for the time being. Affordable supply first and foremost," he said in response.

Robertson said the goal of doubling housing starts was based on the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp.'s estimates of the supply gap, or the number of homes the country needed to add to restore affordability to 2019 levels.

Hitting that annual pace requires the private sector to build at scale, he said, adding the government is "doing everything" it can to stabilize markets like Toronto and Vancouver that are struggling to get shovels in the ground.

The minister said the government has made "unprecedented" interventions to stimulate construction, including moves to axe the GST on many newly built units and other federal incentives to get municipalities to lower costly development charges.

But "the Government of Canada cannot force Canadians to build housing," he said.

"Right now we're doing everything that we can in a very challenging time for our economy," Robertson said.

"We have to continue focusing on where we intervene, working with provinces and cities to get them building as much as possible and looking at the affordable side. That's where the role of government is, to make sure there's affordable housing getting built."

Non-market housing is usually more affordable and relies on government support to get built — but those homes account for only a small share of the overall number of units built in a year.

Conservative housing critic Scott Aitchison accused the Liberals of quietly dropping their homebuilding target and moving the goalposts.

"Their big promises have become another Liberal housing illusion. Tripling the speed of slow is still unbearably slow and will not make homes affordable again," he said in a media statement on Tuesday.

In its fall housing supply report, the CMHC wrote that the country is entering a "new phase" where slowing population growth is leading to more balance in Canadian rental markets.

But the Crown corporation warned that the annual pace of housing starts is well short of levels needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability to the market in the next 10 years.

The CMHC's "business-as-usual" forecast sees Canada breaking ground on 231,000 homes per year, which it estimates would leave the market up to 238,000 homes short of affordable levels by 2036.

Affordability will remain out of reach if Canada fails to take advantage of this moment to rapidly build housing supply ahead of the next surge in demand, the CMHC said.

Experts point out that many of the levers to increase housing supply are outside the government's direct control, such as Bank of Canada interest rates and the cost of building materials.

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Institute, told The Canadian Press last week that he never liked the goal of doubling housing starts because it could be "excessive" and lacks a nuanced approach to the mix of homes Canada must build.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The Canadian real estate correction is already the largest in history, and gets even bigger after inflation. It's not over, according to BMO.
items.body:
Canadian real estate’s historic price correction is slowing down, but the pain may not be over. In a research note to investors, BMO Capital Markets explains it’s even larger in real terms. The banks warn that the math doesn’t work out in favour of households, who are still struggling with affordability. Combined with the recent upward pressure on interest rates, they see real home prices falling further for at least another year.

Canadian Home Price Declines Slowing After Historic Drop

The historic correction for Canadian home prices isn’t over, but it is losing steam. Price declines are getting smaller, with another bank even declaring the bottom. “Canadian home prices appear to be nearly flattening out in nominal terms, but the adjustment is ongoing after accounting for inflation—and we suspect it will continue,” says BMO Economist Robert Kavcic.

The latest national benchmark from CREA shows a typical home has shed 22.8% (-$191.6k) from the March 2022 peak. In the past year, the benchmark fell 3.1% (-$20.7k), a relatively small move in contrast to the $649.9k benchmark. However, those declines are in nominal terms. In real (inflation-adjusted) terms, the market is a whole different story.

Canadians Have Seen Inflation Run Hot—and It’s Not Slowing Down

October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) report shows prices are 3.1% higher than last year, over 50% higher than the BoC target. Consumer prices have grown 19.9% from 2020 to 2025, or 3.7% annualized over the 5 years. Significantly outpacing the target inflation rate means stronger depreciation in real terms.

“Real Canadian home prices are down 4.7% from a year ago after inflation, and are now down a massive 20% from five years ago— that’s the steepest five-year real decline on record going back to the start of the 1980s,” notes Kavcic.

Canadian Home Prices Not Expected To Rise Through 2030

Inflation-adjusted average Canadian home price.

Source: BMO Capital Markets; CREA.

One may assume the sharpest drop in history means the market is ready to return? Not exactly.

“Given where valuations still sit relative to income and rent, and assuming that interest rates are nudging higher rather than headed lower, there is simply no scope for price increases to run ahead of inflation at this stage,” warns Kavcic.

He’s not outright dismissing the possibility of an uptick in home prices. The math is just working against it, especially when it comes to real terms.

“Thus, even if nominal prices turn the corner, the adjustment relative to inflation (and, similarly, relative to household income) will continue in the year (or more) ahead,” warns Kavcic.

items.title: Canadian consumer confidence stalls as homeowners grow more cautious
items.description: Homeowner mood dips in Nanos data weeks after the Bank of Canada rate hike
items.content: <p>Homeowner mood dips in Nanos data weeks after the Bank of Canada rate hike</p><img src="https://ca.res.keymedia.com/files/image/iStock-housinghomemortgage(500%20x%20333).jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Homeowner mood dips in Nanos data weeks after the Bank of Canada rate hike
items.body:
Canadian consumer confidence spent the past month going nowhere, and the latest data suggest homeowners are now less upbeat than the renters down the street.

The Bloomberg Nanos Canadian Confidence Index (BNCCI) registered 51.54 for the four weeks ending November 13. That was barely changed from 51.68 a month earlier and well short of its 54.64 average since tracking began in 2008, according to Nanos Research Corporation.

A reading of 50 means positive and negative views cancel each other out.

The tracking window included the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision to lift its overnight rate to 2.5%. It was the central bank’s first increase since 2023. A year ago, the index sat at 48.63. 

What the housing outlook means for mortgage brokers

Roughly 32% of Canadians expect home values in their neighbourhood to rise over the next six months. That is up from 29% four weeks earlier but below this year’s 34% average and the 40% long-run norm. Another 21% expect prices to fall.

The Expectations Index, which blends views on the economy and real estate, sat at 48.75, still net negative.

That caution matches recent bank forecasts. TD expects home sales and prices to decline through the fourth quarter. Economist Rishi Sondhi warned that “the risk is that November is another subdued month for housing.” 

The broader index briefly slipped below the neutral mark in September before recovering in October. It has averaged 51.06 so far in 2026, according to Nanos.

Shaun Cathcart and Garry Bhaura of CREA, Michael Davenport of Oxford Economics, and Sherry Cooper of Dominion Lending Centres Group say higher rates and economic uncertainty are keeping Canada's housing market subdued. https://t.co/3C37E4W4gQ — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 18, 2026

Why are homeowners less confident than renters?

Sentiment among homeowners slipped to 50.14 from 51.64 four weeks earlier, edging toward net-negative territory. Renters climbed to 54.81 from 51.90 over the same period.

Ontario scored 49.57 and the Prairies came in at 49.81, the only two regions below neutral. British Columbia moved the other way, jumping to 53.56 from 46.02 four weeks earlier. Quebec posted the strongest regional reading at 53.70.

Household balance sheets remain the weak spot. Only 9% of respondents said their personal finances improved over the past year, against 42% who said they were worse off.

Job security held up better, with 66% describing their work as secure or somewhat secure, above the 2026 average of 63%. Fewer than 6% said their jobs were not secure at all or somewhat not secure.

How Canadians see their neighbourhood housing market

Bloomberg Nanos Canadian Confidence Index, four weeks ending November 13, 2026

Source: Nanos Research for Bloomberg; random telephone survey of 1,019 Canadians aged 18 and over, four-week rolling average ending November 13, 2026. Margin of error ±3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

items._ogDesc: Western Canada's mortgage industry gathers in Vancouver in February for its annual summit
items.body:
Vancouver Convention Centre will play host to the Canadian Mortgage Summit Vancouver on February 25, 2027, as mortgage brokers, lenders, underwriters, and industry service providers from across Western Canada converge for a full day of market intelligence, business strategy, and lending solutions.

The event marks the latest edition of a conference series built specifically around the challenges and opportunities facing mortgage professionals in British Columbia and the broader western region.

A market in transition

The timing of the 2027 summit reflects the conditions reshaping Canadian mortgage brokering. Broker market share has climbed to 33% of new residential mortgage originations, up four percentage points since the end of 2022, according to CMP's 2026 Brokers on Lenders report.

The program has been designed to address this environment directly. The agenda is organised around four themes:

  1. Market intelligence - covering changing conditions and borrower behaviour across Western Canada;
  2. Artificial intelligence and technology - examining how automation and digital tools can sharpen broker workflows;
  3. Business strategy and growth - focusing on adaptation and diversification in a tighter market;
  4. Lending solutions - exploring private, mortgage investment corporation (MIC), and alternative financing structures

Western Canada carries its own dynamics. British Columbia's housing market has been under consistent affordability pressure, and brokers operating in the province face a client base navigating some of Canada's highest property values alongside elevated interest rate sensitivity.

For the alternative lending sector in particular, British Columbia and Alberta represent two of the most active markets for private mortgage activity, a fact reflected in the sponsor roster assembled for the 2027 event.

Speakers and what attendees can expect

The confirmed speaker lineup spans origination, alternative lending, technology, and mortgage education.

Joe White, founder of Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC) and IMBoundless, is among the featured presenters.

White, a Canadian Mortgage Professional Hall of Fame inductee, has trained more than 50,000 mortgage students and leads what the organization describes as Canada's largest mortgage and insurance education platform.

Jared Stanley, chief operating officer at Neighbourhood Holdings in British Columbia, will also appear. Stanley oversaw the alternative lender's growth to $2 billion in volume by April 2025 and has spoken publicly about the role of process automation and AI-assisted underwriting in scaling complex file management.

Neighbourhood Holdings completed the acquisition of Fisgard Asset Management in October 2025, a deal that positions the combined entity as one of Canada's larger alternative lenders.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthONE Bank of Canada, brings more than 20 years of mortgage and financial services experience to the program.

Armstrong leads origination strategy and broker channel development at WealthONE, which specializes in lending solutions for self-employed borrowers, multiple property owners, and newcomers to Canada — borrower profiles that represent a significant and growing share of broker deal flow in British Columbia.

Michael Wolfe, vice president of residential lending at EQ Bank (a subsidiary of Equitable Bank), and Ryan Spence, principal of broker channel development at Filogix, round out the confirmed roster, with additional speakers expected to be announced in the weeks ahead.

The Canadian Mortgage Summit Vancouver is currently accepting waitlist registrations ahead of a broader registration opening. Sponsorship opportunities remain available. 

Full event details and waitlist registration are available at vancouver.canadianmortgagesummit.com.
