items.description: Canada's largest mortgage educator on recognition, trust, and what the CMAs mean for the next generation
items.content: <p>Canada's largest mortgage educator on recognition, trust, and what the CMAs mean for the next generation</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639256797300291475.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada's largest mortgage educator on recognition, trust, and what the CMAs mean for the next generation
items.body:
Joe White (pictured top) has trained most of the people competing at this year's Canadian Mortgage Awards. The founder and chief executive of the Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC) in Toronto has licensed more than 20,000 mortgage professionals in Ontario alone since founding the company in 2008, and each year REMIC trains more than 15,000 students across financial services.

When the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards return to Rebel Toronto on November 25, marking the programme's 20th anniversary, many of the finalists will have started their careers in one of his classrooms.

Seeing the full journey

"When I look at the finalist list, I see a lot of people who started in one of our classrooms," White told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"Sponsoring the awards lets us see that whole path, from the first day of licensing to standing on a stage being recognised by their peers."

The awards, presented by Canadian Mortgage Professional, span 23 competitive categories this year, from individual broker performance to brokerage innovation and technology.

The ceremony will be hosted by broadcaster Sonia Mangat and winners will be announced the same night across CMP's channels.

REMIC is backing the FinFluencer of the Year award in particular, a category recognising brokers who build a public profile online and educate Canadian consumers about mortgages and financial products.

The recognition, he argues, sets a standard that advertising alone cannot. "When new agents see what excellence looks like, they have something to aim for," he said.

"And frankly, our industry needs to make the case for the value of professional, licensed advice now more than ever."

White sees the category as a natural fit for an organisation whose newest programs encourage licensees to establish a digital presence from the moment they qualify.

"The brokers who are building trust online and educating Canadians in public are doing work that matters," he said, "and they deserve a spotlight."

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is proud to partner with RPS in recognizing the Excellence Awardees of the RPS Award for Brokerage/Team of the Year (25 Employees or More). #MortgageAwardsCA Book a table: https://t.co/DpeOmLlH9a https://t.co/2TA4fmH933 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 17, 2026

Why recognition matters now

White's argument for the awards goes beyond ceremony. The public, he says, does not see what a skilled broker actually does — they see a rate.

They do not see the broker who salvaged a self-employed client's deal at nine in the evening, or the agent who talked a family out of a mortgage they could not afford. Recognition, he believes, corrects that.

"Because the public doesn't see what good brokers do," White said.

"Recognition sets the standard. When new agents see what excellence looks like, they have something to aim for. And frankly, our industry needs to make the case for the value of professional, licensed advice now more than ever."

That case is becoming more urgent. A national survey commissioned by REMIC and conducted by Abacus Data in June found that among Canadians aged 18 to 29, more had used AI tools for financial or mortgage advice in the past year — 26% — than had used a licensed mortgage broker or financial adviser — 17%.

Nearly half of all Canadians surveyed did not know whether AI mortgage advice was regulated. Trust still favours the licensed professional, but White is clear-eyed about the direction of travel.

The brokers most visible in 2027, he said, will be the ones who explain things clearly, show up where consumers are looking, and use technology to serve clients better.

items.title: Canadian Mortgage Awards: EQ Bank supports reverse mortgage excellence
items.description: Executive on broker advice, education and opportunity in reverse mortgage lending heading into 2027
items.content: <p>Executive on broker advice, education and opportunity in reverse mortgage lending heading into 2027</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_639306232636088373.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Executive on broker advice, education and opportunity in reverse mortgage lending heading into 2027
items.body:
Reverse mortgages are playing an increasingly important role in Canada’s mortgage landscape – and next week’s Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) will recognize the broker who’s made the most outstanding contribution to that sector over the past year.

The Broker of the Year – Reverse Mortgages award, sponsored by EQ Bank, is one of 23 shortlisted awards up for grabs on November 25 at Rebel Toronto, with this year marking a landmark 20th anniversary for Canada’s most prestigious mortgage industry awards.

Prakash Bector, vice president of sales and distribution at EQ Bank, told Canadian Mortgage Professional the sponsorship reflects the company’s commitment to recognizing excellence within the reverse space.

“We’re proud to support the Canadian Mortgage Awards because they celebrate the people and organizations that continue to raise the bar across our industry,” he said. “It’s an area where great advice and education can make a meaningful difference for Canadians, and we’re excited to recognize the brokers doing exceptional work.”

Originations in the reverse mortgage sector have soared over the past decade as Canadians over the age of 55 increasingly view it as a viable means of tapping into existing home equity.

Bector said brokers have played an essential part in growing the reach and prominence of reverse mortgages across the country.

Brokers’ role as a conduit between lender and borrower has been key to that surge. “Our industry is built on relationships, trust and advice,” Bector said. “Brokers play an important role in helping Canadians navigate increasingly complex financial decisions, often at major points in their lives.

“Recognizing excellence gives us an opportunity to celebrate the people who are innovating, adapting and delivering great outcomes for their clients while continuing to move our industry forward.”

Three of Canada’s preeminent brokers in the reverse mortgage market are up for this year’s Broker of the Year – Reverse Mortgages honour.

Excellence Awardees for 2026 are Parminder Bhatti of AKAL Mortgages Inc., Rich Ulvild of Xeva Mortgage, and Yamini Mehta of 8Twelve Mortgage Corp.

Advice in a challenging market

The housing and mortgage markets have faced plenty of familiar challenges in 2026, including an uncertain economic environment and rising interest rates. But Bector said those difficult conditions have underlined the value of industry expertise and client service – with the brokers who focus on those fundamentals setting themselves in good stead for the coming years.

“It’s been a challenging market, but I think it has also reinforced the value of great advice,” he said. “Looking ahead to 2027, I see a lot of opportunity for brokers who stay close to their clients and think beyond the traditional mortgage transaction.”

It’s been a tough ask for many brokers to eke out new business in 2026 with plenty of potential buyers and borrowers remaining on the sidelines, but Bector said existing client relationships can prove a potent resource for brokers as they map out their plan for the coming months.

With those connections, Bector said, the value of the advice and expertise brokers can provide comes to the fore. “There are opportunities within the relationships and databases brokers already have,” he said.

“Whether it’s helping a client with an alternative lending solution, accessing equity in their home or simply approaching their financial needs differently, the brokers who ask the right questions and understand their clients more deeply will continue to differentiate themselves.”

Education, relationships to the fore for EQ Bank

Helping provide brokers with the tools and guidance they need to best advise Canadians on reverse mortgage opportunities has been top of mind for EQ Bank this year, according to Bector.

An educational approach has been central to that strategy. “That means continuing to strengthen our alternative and reverse mortgage businesses, investing in education and broker partnerships, and making it easier for brokers to have broader conversations with their clients.

“Ultimately, we want EQB to be a partner brokers can turn to when the answer isn’t obvious and help them find a path forward.”

items.title: OIM Group CEO on why the Canadian Mortgage Awards matter
items.description: Teddy Kyres backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as the industry heads into a pivotal year for brokers
items.content: <p>Teddy Kyres backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as the industry heads into a pivotal year for brokers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639306209440117745.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Teddy Kyres backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as the industry heads into a pivotal year for brokers
items.body:
As the Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) prepare for their 20th anniversary ceremony on November 25 at Rebel Toronto, one of the event's sponsors is making the case for why recognition matters as much as performance in a business where isolation can be an occupational hazard.

Teddy Kyres (pictured top), CEO of The OIM Group in Montreal, says the independent broker community works hard, and rarely stops to take stock of that. For him, backing the CMAs is not simply a marketing decision. It is a conviction about what the industry owes its people.

"I've always believed that the people who make this industry successful are the brokers themselves, and I don't think they always get the recognition they deserve," Kyres told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"Mortgage brokering can be a very independent and sometimes isolating business."

According to Mortgage Professionals Canada's 2026 consumer survey, the share of Canadians who obtained their mortgage through a broker climbed to 38% in 2026, up six percentage points from the year before.

Despite that growth, Kyres argues the channel's contribution is still undervalued in the public imagination.

"Mortgage brokers play a much bigger role in the Canadian economy than they're often given credit for," he said.

"We're helping Canadians make some of the biggest financial decisions of their lives, supporting homeownership, and playing an important role in the overall housing and financial markets. Yet I don't think the general public always understands the amount of work, knowledge, and responsibility that goes into being a good mortgage broker."

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is proud to recognize the Excellence Awardees of the MCAN Award for Woman of Distinction, presented in partnership with MCAN. #MortgageAwardsCA Book a table: https://t.co/ob1RgVgGjc https://t.co/rLUBoZs9g2 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 18, 2026

A year of challenge and change

The backdrop to this year's ceremony is a mortgage market shaped by sustained economic pressure.

The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) projects that approximately 1.15 million mortgages will renew in 2026, the largest concentration of renewal activity in recent history. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) has also flagged "mortgage payment shocks" as a key risk for the year ahead.

Kyres does not minimise the difficulty.

"I think 2026 has been a challenging year for brokers in many parts of Canada," he said.

"There has been a lot of economic uncertainty, changing market conditions, and things that are simply outside of our control. What we can control is how hard we work, how we run our businesses, and how we take care of our clients."

For OIM, the year has also been one of significant structural growth.

Formed through a joint venture between Orbis Mortgage Group and Indi Mortgage in January, The OIM Group quickly established itself as one of the largest national independent brokerage platforms in Canada, now supporting more than 800 mortgage professionals across its family of brands.

Alongside Orbis and Indi, the platform includes the Independent Mortgage Network (IMN), in-house alternative lender Swyft Mortgage, a national underwriting desk, an OIM Rewards programme, and a broker pension and retirement plan — the first brokerage-contributed pension model of its kind in Canada.

"We've spent a lot of time challenging the traditional way things are done in our industry," Kyres said.

"Just because something has always been done a certain way doesn't mean it's the best way to do it."

Technology, relationships, and what comes next

Looking ahead to 2027, Kyres is measured about the pace of change ahead.

Artificial intelligence and automation are already reshaping origination workflows, and he expects that pressure to accelerate over the next two to three years.

His view is that the brokers who adapt earliest will gain the most, but that the foundational value of the channel remains unchanged.

"Technology and AI are going to make us faster, more efficient, and change the way we operate," he said.

"Brokers who embrace those changes will have an advantage, but I firmly believe that the relationships we build will remain the most important part of our business. Your clients, your referral sources, and your reputation are what allow you to grow and build a sustainable business."

For the CMAs specifically, Kyres sees the awards as one mechanism by which the industry can raise its own standards — not simply by naming winners, but by making excellence visible across the channel.

"If we don't recognise and promote the value of our own industry, who will?" he said.

"Recognition is not just about winning awards. It's about building credibility, raising standards, and making sure the mortgage broker channel continues to grow and earn the respect it deserves."

The full shortlist across 23 categories is available at canadianmortgageawards.com.

items.title: Choice Properties REIT Buys Royal Oak Wholesale Club In Burnaby For $38.5M
items.description:
Toronto-based Choice Properties REIT (TSX: CHP.UN) has acquired a Wholesale Club at a prominent intersection in Burnaby, British Columbia, and the site is primed for redevelopment.

The Wholesale is located at 5335 Kingsway near the intersection with Royal Oak Avenue in the Royal Oak neighbourhood, a few blocks north from the Expo Line SkyTrain’s Royal Oak Station.

The 2.84-acre property is occupied by a Wholesale Club, a Costco-like chain owned by Loblaw Companies Limited, which is in turn owned by George Weston Limited.

On September 8, Choice Properties REIT acquired 5335 Kingsway for $38,500,000, according to the REIT’s Q3 2026 report published last week. The transaction closed for a total of $39,731,000 when including related costs. The vendor was Arbutus Properties Ltd.

BC Assessment values 5335 Kingsway at $40,153,000 in its latest assessment, which is dated to July 1, 2025.

Loblaw Companies is the largest unitholder in Choice Properties REIT and also one of its major tenants.

The acquisition represents the largest acquisition the REIT has made in 2026, and Loblaw now represents 57.1% of the REIT’s rental revenue.

The Property

The 5335 Kingsway property has been on the market for over a year now, after being listed for sale last summer by Kevin Douglas, Edgar Buksevics, Kevin Meikle, and Colton Zayshley of JLL on an unpriced basis.

Last spring, the City of Burnaby approved the Royal Oak Community Plan, laying the groundwork for the neighbourhood to be redeveloped, with the intersection of Royal Oak Avenue and Kingsway being identified as the key “Village Centre Node.”

The Village Centre Node consists of only a few properties at the northeast corner of the intersection, one of which is 5335 Kingsway. Under the Royal Oak Community Plan, the site can accommodate high-rise development up to 30 storeys.

A preliminary conceptual development for 5335 Kingsway in Burnaby. (Arcadis, JLL)

The property was marketed by JLL with that development potential in mind, with JLL saying in their sales brochure that “the property’s size accommodates various development options including multiple towers, retail space, and diverse amenities.”

“An additional 10 storeys are available through the City of Burnaby’s Community Benefit Bonus Policy, increasing potential heights up to maximum of 40 storeys,” JLL added. “Conceptual plans for 5335 Kingsway envision 1,028,463 sf of developable area and 8.32 FSR under the base 30 storey zoning, across a 3 tower mixed-use built form.”

The real estate market is still amidst a downturn, but the Wholesale Club — the building being 47,775 sq. ft — “provides consistent interim holding income to the Property while developers work through entitlements and development vision.”

Choice Properties REIT

Although its primary focus is retail, Choice Properties REIT is also a developer now that large retail properties have become prime for intensification.

Over in Coquitlam, at the boundary with Burnaby, Choice Properties REIT has partnered with Vancouver-based developer Wesgroup to redevelop 439 and 465 North Road — a Denny’s and the Cariboo Centre retail plaza — into a master-planned community with six high-rise towers, as previously reported by STOREYS.

Earlier this year, Choice Properties REIT partnered with Toronto-based private equity real estate investment firm KingSett Capital to acquire First Capital REIT (TSX: FCR.UN) in a $9.4 billion deal.

According to Choice’s Q3 report, both First Capital REIT’s unitholders and the Ontario Superior Court gave their stamp of approval for the deal in June and the transaction is expected to close in Q4 2026 or Q1 2027.

As for Q3, the REIT reported that their occupancy rate was 91.4% for mixed-use and residential properties, 97.5% for retail properties, and 98.6% for industrial properties. Funds From Operations (FFO) per unit diluted grew by 2.2% year over year and is now $0.284 while same-asset net operating income grew by 3.1%.

items.title: Chief AI officers lack control over AI spending: study
items.description: ‘Few leaders have a broader view of how AI is creating value across the enterprise'
items.content: <p>‘Few leaders have a broader view of how AI is creating value across the enterprise'</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/036/0363_639305287670257804.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: ‘Few leaders have a broader view of how AI is creating value across the enterprise'
items.body:
Most chief AI officers can see where artificial intelligence is paying off in their organizations, but few have the authority to act on it, according to a global study released by the IBM Institute for Business Value. 

That gap leaves the decisions that shape jobs, skills and how work gets redesigned with other executives, putting people leaders at the centre of whether AI delivers.

The study surveyed 1,667 chief AI officers (CAIOs) and equivalent enterprise AI leaders across 33 geographies and 20 industries from April to June 2026. Only 18% said they have full control over AI investment decisions, and just 15% have full authority over AI workforce strategy. 

Three-quarters of Canadian AI leaders surveyed say their organizations risk falling behind competitors in AI transformation, yet only 15% have full authority over AI investment decisions.

Joanne Wright, senior vice-president of transformation and operations at IBM, summed up the bind in the report’s foreword: “Few leaders have a broader view of how AI is creating value across the enterprise. Yet the outcomes they are accountable for often depend on decisions made by others.”

A fast-growing role in Canada

The bind matters because the role is spreading fast. IBM’s 2026 CEO Study found 76% of organizations now have someone in the role, up from 26% in 2025.

In Canada, separate IBM research of 160 executives found 81% of organizations surveyed have a CAIO, The Logic reported in June 2026. 

As of June 2026, Scotiabank had no CAIO, while OMERS, PSP Investments and BCI had placed AI with the chief technology officer, The Logic reported.

The CHRO partnership gap

Wherever the role sits, CAIOs cannot redesign work alone, the report says. It urges them to partner with the chief human resources officer (CHRO) to evolve existing roles, or create new ones, for AI-first workflows, and to update incentives to reward AI-enabled outcomes.

Many Canadian employers are not there yet. An IBM study with Oxford Economics found HR is left out of AI strategy at 37% of Canadian firms, while TD research on Canada’s widening AI skills gap shows the workforce stakes. 

Governance adds friction. While 48% of CAIOs said AI agents initiate and execute actions across workflows, 75% said governance, risk or compliance delays AI-driven action. Only 61% said AI decision rights are clearly defined and consistently applied.

What high-impact AI leaders do differently

Some organizations have found a way through. IBM identified a group of high-impact CAIOs whose organizations report stronger results: 63% of their AI projects deliver measurable business outcomes, versus 43% elsewhere, and they scale initiatives enterprise-wide in eight months rather than 13.5. The data is self-reported and shows association, not cause.

The clearest difference is financial discipline. Some 96% of these leaders cut or stop funding for underperforming AI initiatives, even with senior sponsorship, compared with 46% of others.

“We stop when the value isn’t there,” said Pascal Belaud, executive vice-president and chief AI and data officer at Truist.

What should a chief AI officer be?

That discipline points to the kind of leader the report describes. Wright wrote that successful AI leadership “requires more than technical expertise or operational oversight,” adding: “It requires gathering evidence, influencing decisions, and measuring success.”

IBM’s action guides show what that means in practice. CAIOs should define which decisions AI can make and which need human judgment, redesign high-value workflows end-to-end around AI, and manage AI as a portfolio, funding what works and stopping what doesn’t.

“The CAIO job is more of an education job than people realize,” said Abhi Seth, chief data and AI officer at The Boeing Company, in the report.

Without authority over workforce strategy, the CAIO’s influence depends on the CHRO.

items.body:
Han Lee says making and answering client calls is one of his biggest challenges as a Realtor, often leaving little time for himself and his family.

So he and his business partners built an AI receptionist that’s on call 24 hours a day.

Their software uses AI to answer incoming phone calls and take down clients’ information and requests. Initially built for his own business, the system is now being offered to other real estate companies.

“As a one-person Realtor or a one-person owner of the business, there's only so much you can do,” said Burnaby-based Lee, owner of the JulyWork administrative software tool.

The system connects to the company’s calendar and can book appointments with Realtors based on their availability, areas of expertise and language skills, according to Lee.

“Our ‘receptionist’ … can pick up to 100 calls at a time,” he said, adding that the team developed it so the voice sounds like a real person.

Lee said AI can also identify highly specific property features that would otherwise require Realtors to manually review individual listings and photographs.

“It is so smart that it can search very weird and sophisticated things that people will never be able to really do,” he said.

Human connection hard to replace

Mike Stewart, a Vancouver-based Realtor and real estate blogger, said AI has become increasingly integrated into his work over the past few years, particularly for writing property listings, creating marketing content and conducting research.

However, he sees AI as most useful for time-consuming administrative and back-end tasks, allowing Realtors to focus on the most important part of their job — connecting with clients.

“And so then time is freed up for the Realtor to spend more time generating business by speaking to people or following up with past clients to strengthen the relationships,” he said.

While AI can identify properties that match a buyer’s stated requirements, Stewart said it cannot always anticipate a client’s potential needs in the same way an experienced Realtor can.

“We're dealing with human nature, and so often the journey of buying a property often takes a path that is not predictable initially,” said Stewart.

For example, a client who originally wants a two-level red house may end up buying a four-storey blue house, he said.

“So much of what we do is helping the clients understand how a house may work for their lives and supporting them with that,” said Stewart.

“And it's very much a subjective feel type of thing where the people go into the house, they see it and they feel it. And there's limits to what an artificial intelligence can do to help them with the feel.”

Marketing content shows up in AI search

As more buyers turn to AI platforms to search for properties and real estate services, companies should pay greater attention to the content they publish online to improve their visibility in AI-generated answers, according to Gerardo Bonilla, co-founder and CEO at Temso AI.

His marketing firm, which helps businesses improve their visibility in AI-generated search results, analyzed around 80,000 source citations for the luxury real estate industry and released a report in October.

One of the main findings was that Google AI Mode drew about 83 per cent of their citations from commercial websites, said Bonilla. The report found similar results across other AI platforms, including 77 per cent for Google AI Overviews, 80 per cent for Gemini and 79 per cent for ChatGPT.

“That [means] most of the sources in the way that [AI] weighs who to trust when it comes to answering these questions come from commercial websites,” said Bonilla.

“What that means specifically for brands is that in this industry, their content on their website matters a lot.”

Those sources can include real estate agencies publishing their own content, as well as resellers and comparison websites, he added.

Although the algorithms behind AI-generated answers remain difficult to understand fully, Bonilla said real estate companies can take steps to improve the likelihood that their websites will be cited.

These include ensuring AI citation bots can access their websites, and publishing content in a format that makes it easier for AI systems to identify and reference relevant information.

“For example, AI citation bots love primary data. So if there's any primary data that you have, then you can be publishing,” he said.

He also recommended that companies write in a way that they're answering the question in full in a very specific way.

“So humans, we tend to be able to ‘read between the lines,’ whereas AI citation bots prefer writing that is a lot more explicit,” said Bonilla.

“So the more explicit you are and the more in-depth you answer a certain topic, the likelier you are to basically get picked up by an agent.”

items._ogDesc: October home sales crept up slightly from the previous month but were still down more than 10 per cent from a year ago, the Canadian Real Estate Association said in its latest report Tuesday. Home sales last month totalled 37,827, down 10.
items.body:
October home sales crept up slightly from the previous month but were still down more than 10 per cent from a year ago, the Canadian Real Estate Association said in its latest report Tuesday.

Home sales last month totalled 37,827, down 10.6 per cent from October 2025. But on a seasonally adjusted basis, activity edged up 0.3 per cent compared with September.

“Despite most forecasters sharpening their pencils and lowering their predictions, so far we’ve only seen a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, probably less than many would have predicted in an environment of rising interest rates,” Garry Bhaura, CREA's chair, said in a news release.

“With the market moving into its traditionally quieter months, now is a great time to shift into planning mode for 2027."

The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month — the first hike in more than three years — to reduce the risk that stubbornly high oil prices become persistent inflation.

The move prompted Canada's big banks to raise their benchmark prime rates, pushing the amount charged on variable rate mortgages higher.

A summary of deliberations released earlier this month by the central bank also suggested its governing council thinks it might need to raise rates further, but will proceed carefully.

Michael Davenport, senior economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a report Tuesday that Canada's resale housing market had a quiet October and is heading into "hibernation" for the winter.

"Rising mortgage rates, a soft labour market and elevated job insecurity from the trade war with the United States will likely cause housing demand to weaken in the near term, pushing home sales and prices modestly lower before a tepid recovery gets underway next spring," he wrote.

"We don’t expect the recent softness in the housing market to deter the (Bank of Canada) from hiking ... to 2.75 per cent in December."

Meanwhile, CREA said the national average sale price in October ticked down 1.6 per cent from a year ago to $678,584.

New listings fell 5.5 per cent to 75,814, but on a seasonally adjusted basis, were up 0.8 per cent from the month before and outpaced sales activity.

CREA said there were about 197,000 properties listed for sale on all Canadian MLS systems at the end of October, up slightly from the long-term average of 190,000.

It said there were five months of inventory on a national basis at the end of October, up slightly from the summer.

Cailey Heaps, CEO at Heaps Estrin Real Estate Team in Toronto, said deals are coming together when sellers have realistic expectations about pricing and buyers are willing to act.

The segment that's been the most challenging has been for properties that are "family homes" to be lived in long-term.

"Those people are currently housed, so they don't feel any pressure to act. They want to take a bit of a wait-and-see approach," she said.

"The first-time buyer market is very active — incredibly active."

Heaps is expecting a "fairly flat" market through the winter as concern over job security and tariffs weigh on confidence.

"And then I do think that spring will start to see an uptick, not only in pricing but also in volume."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate’s has one of the largest corrections in history and it’s still going, as buyers balked at this price level in October.
items.body:
Canadian real estate has made one of the sharpest corrections on record, and it’s still going. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows prices fell further in October. Weak demand and lofty inventory suggest that buyers are still balking at this level. Over 4 years in a correction have only rolled back 13 months of 2020’s low rate, speculative boom.

Canada’s Housing Correction Reversed 13 Months of Gains

The price of a typical home across Canada.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home slipped 0.3% (-$2.1k) to $649.9k in October, 3.1% (-$20.7k) lower than last year. Prices are now 22.8% (-$191.6k) lower than the March 2022 peak, and sit just a little higher than they were back in February 2021. Nearly half a decade of correcting, and most Canadians still couldn’t afford to buy, even if they wanted to.

Canadian Home Sales Fall, Remain Historically Weak

Canadian home sales on the MLS in October.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

There was an abrupt drop in home sales last month. Only 37.8k homes were sold in October, 10.6% fewer than last year and marks a 3-year low. That doesn’t sound bad, but excluding the slowdown since 2022, this level was last seen in 2012. Home sales are better than they were at the start of the downturn, but are still hovering around levels seen in the wake of the global financial crisis.

Canadian Home Sellers Still Flooding The Market

New listings of homes for sale on the Canadian MLS, October.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The inventory side weakened too—just not as much as it did when it comes to home sales. CREA reported 75.8k new listings in October, 5.5% lower than last year, and just a smidge under October 2024. This may be a 3-year low, but October’s new listings have never been this strong before 2020.

A sharper drop in sales left the sales-to-new-listings ratio (SNLR) at 49.9% in October, 2.8 points below last year. The ratio is technically in balanced territory, but this time of year tends to see sellers pull back. The SNLR doesn’t show a buyer’s market, but October hasn’t seen the ratio this low since 2008. In fact, that’s the only October to come in lower in the past three decades.

When does this market downturn end? This is one of the sharpest downturns on record, yet not much progress has been made. The market’s been like a slow-moving car crash, spending over 4 years rolling back just 13 months of gains. Home prices in Canada have always moved fast, but from 2015 to 2022 was another story. Taxpayer-backed incentives helped to grow prices much faster than incomes and credit capacity. The inefficiencies didn’t build up overnight, and they won’t correct overnight either.

items.title: Grechi Carter ready to recognize industry’s finest at the CMAs
items.description: Daniele Grechi, a partner at the firm, tells CMP why supporting this year’s crop of commercial brokers is more important than ever
items.content: <p>Daniele Grechi, a partner at the firm, tells CMP why supporting this year’s crop of commercial brokers is more important than ever</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639294998909890808.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Daniele Grechi, a partner at the firm, tells CMP why supporting this year’s crop of commercial brokers is more important than ever
items.body:
With just days remaining until one of the most anticipated events in Canada’s mortgage industry calendar, Excellence Awardees and their teams are gearing up for what’s sure to be an unforgettable night at the Canadian Mortgage Awards at Rebel Toronto (November 25).

The event – now entering its 20th year – wouldn’t be the same without the involvement of the award sponsors, who play a crucial role in supporting and recognizing the best and brightest in the mortgage industry.

Toronto real estate law firm Grechi Carter Professional Corporation will present the award for Broker of the Year – Commercial next week, and Daniele Grechi (pictured top), a partner at the firm, told Canadian Mortgage Professional that supporting the event marks a natural extension of the company’s push into the lending community.

“While Grechi Carter is a full-service real estate law firm, at our core we’re a lending firm,” he said. “Lending represents the majority of our business, extending even to our litigation department, which specializes in mortgage enforcement.”

“As a firm, we’ve made it a priority to deepen our involvement in the lending community, and we view the Canadian Mortgage Awards as the pinnacle of industry recognition.”

The company has developed a strong presence in private lending and among mortgage investment corporations (MICs), which pool investor capital to fund mortgages. Grechi said he views commercial lending as the next frontier.

“Having established a strong presence in the private lending and MIC sectors, we’re particularly excited to broaden our relationships within the commercial lending space,” he said. “Supporting these awards is a natural extension of that commitment.”

Celebrating top performers in an eventful market

The CMAs have taken place during years of market turbulence before – from the financial crash to the COVID-era volatility – and the 2026 event arrives against a backdrop of a cooling mortgage market, affordability struggles, and rising interest rates.

Grechi acknowledged the challenging market, but sounded an optimistic tone on what’s in store. “The past few years have been exceptionally challenging for the mortgage and real estate industries,” he said. “However, we are optimistic that we’re at or near the bottom of this cycle and that better days are ahead.”

Excellence Awardees have been named across more than 20 different categories at this year’s CMAs, with final winners to be announced at the glitzy ceremony next Wednesday.

For Grechi, downturns separate the strongest operators from the rest, and those who continue to navigate the current market challenges are likely to succeed in the long run.

“Periods like these tend to distinguish the most resilient, adaptable and capable professionals in our industry,” he said. “As the market recovers, we believe those who have weathered this storm will be particularly well positioned to capitalize on the opportunities ahead. That makes recognizing excellence in our industry all the more meaningful this year.”

How Grechi Carter has approached 2026

Setting up for success for Grechi Carter in the present market has meant continuing to spend even while the market has been weak, Grechi said. “We’ve continued to invest in our people, expertise and technology throughout this market cycle,” he said.

“In particular, we have developed tailored AI-driven processes to enhance quality control, efficiency and consistency, with the objective of delivering the highest standard of legal service to our lending partners. We believe these investments position us well for the next cycle of growth.”

Seven brokers are shortlisted for the Commercial Broker award: Ahmed Hatata of Green Mortgage Solutions Inc., Alexander Durand of Mcommercial, Jason McNeill of 4Capital Mortgages, Jean Luc Dion of Multi-Prêts Commercial, Jonathan Gagnon of Orbis Mortgage Group, Peter Quinn of Multi-Prêts Commercial, and Stephen Thomas of Mortgage Alliance HALO Mortgage Advisory.

Grechi paid tribute to the industry members who have gone above and beyond for clients in a difficult time for many commercial borrowers. “Those who have successfully navigated this environment have demonstrated tremendous resourcefulness and commitment to their businesses and clients,” he said.

items.title: Canadian Home Sales Inch Up In October As Interest Rates Climb
items.description:
The Canadian housing market barely moved in October, which is a better result than many forecasters expected heading into fall. Home sales on Canadian MLS® Systems rose 0.3% from September, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA).

October also brought a rate hike from the Bank of Canada. CREA doesn’t expect it to turn into a repeat of 2022.

“In a widely expected move, the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate at its October 28 announcement with the goal of tamping down Canadians’ concerns about creeping inflation stemming from higher energy costs,” said Shaun Cathcart, CREA’s Senior Economist. “That said, with the Bank’s preferred inflation measures still very well behaved, this is unlikely to be a repeat of the 2022 tightening cycle. Rather, it is more likely to be of the mild to moderate variety, although that distinction does carry extra weight in times of stretched affordability.”

So far, buyers haven’t pulled back much. “Despite most forecasters sharpening their pencils and lowering their predictions, so far we’ve only seen a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, probably less than many would have predicted in an environment of rising interest rates,” said Garry Bhaura, CREA Chair.

The year-over-year comparison is weaker. Actual (not seasonally adjusted) sales were 10.6% lower than in October 2025.

New listings grew 0.8% month-over-month. Listings rose a little faster than sales did, so the national sales-to-new listings ratio slipped to 48.7% from 49% in September. That’s under the long-term average of 54.7%, but still within the 45% to 65% band CREA associates with a balanced market.

There were roughly 197,000 properties listed for sale nationwide at the end of October, slightly above the long-term average of 190,000. At this point in the year, inventory has ranged from 100,000 listings in fall 2021, when the COVID-19 housing boom was at its peak, to 250,000 a little over a decade ago.

Measured in time, the market had five months of inventory at the end of October. That’s up slightly from the summer and exactly in line with the long-term average. By CREA’s measure, a seller’s market sits below 3.6 months and a buyer’s market sits above 6.4 months.

On prices, the National Composite MLS® Home Price Index (HPI) rose 0.1% from September. CREA said that gain could reasonably be called flat, or the biggest monthly increase in two years.

On an annual basis, the non-seasonally adjusted HPI was 3.1% below October 2025. That’s a smaller drop than September’s and smaller than most of the readings so far in 2026.

The non-seasonally adjusted national average home price came in at $678,584, which is 1.6% lower than a year earlier.

The slow season is next. “With the market moving into its traditionally quieter months, now is a great time to shift into planning mode for 2027,” said Bhaura.

CREA will release its next set of statistics on Tuesday, December 15, 2026.

items.title: How AI is making brokers more powerful
items.description: Top broker on why artificial intelligence is an invaluable tool for brokers – not a threat
items.content: <p>Top broker on why artificial intelligence is an invaluable tool for brokers – not a threat</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639305467499655022.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Top broker on why artificial intelligence is an invaluable tool for brokers – not a threat
items.body:
The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) in the mortgage sector has led t plenty of questions about how the role of mortgage brokers will evolve – but as Streetwise Mortgages founder and Wisely AI co-founder Dalia Barsoum told us at MortgageFest Canada, there are huge opportunities for brokers to utilize the technology to grow and boost their business.

[00:00] This is making us more powerful brokers. AI still needs human judgment. What's effective is to have it do certain things within boundaries but oversee it, train it, and that's where the human touch comes in.

[00:26] Fergal McAlinden: All right. So next up we are joined by Dalia Barsoum who we all know as the founder of Streetwise Mortgages, also coming with a new role this year, co-founder of Wisely AI, which I'm really excited to talk to you about because AI, as we all know, has been a big topic in the industry over the past couple of years. Tell us about Wisely AI. How did the idea come about and what are you guys up to?

[00:49] Dalia Barsoum: So as you know, the market in Ontario and BC shifted, and as a business our revenue got hit and our volume got hit. We had to reinvent ourselves to run leaner so that we can sustain because we don't know how long the runway is, and also to be able to handle more volume once things recover without having to add back our old cost base.

[01:20] That's how the idea started. My co-founder is an engineer and an AI-certified tech geek, and he was basically the one that said, "You know what? Let's find better ways to support the brokerage." That's how the idea came about. How can we integrate AI in our workflow in a smart way, safe way, to be able to handle the volume without adding the cost base and enhance client experience.

[01:49] Fergal McAlinden: It's interesting that you have your eye on when things pick up, which we're hoping will be in the next couple of years. How will the technology that you're developing help brokers once that new wave comes about?

[01:59] Dalia Barsoum: Right now we're integrating AI along the mortgage life cycle, the journey. So from intake to close and nurture, there are opportunities, and every broker is different.

[02:12] For us, we've used AI, we call them AI minions right now. We've used them to enhance our marketing, increase our lead generation, enhance our conversion. We use them to review documents and save time on that front. We also use them to answer the phone and intake from all of our social media channels.

[02:38] The one that we rolled out to the market is the compliance assistant. It's not going to say, "Hey, I've done compliance for you." But it's going to assist you as a principal broker in the process, reducing your time from 40 minutes to 2 minutes and making sure it's surfacing things that you don't see as a human, which we've come across. That's basically what we're doing right now, and we're rolling these minions to the industry, starting with the compliance assistant.

[03:07] Fergal McAlinden: Sounds great. We all remember whenever ChatGPT and other LLMs first gained popularity and there was all this talk about existential threats to certain professions and things like that. I think most people thought about the mortgage industry that it would be a supplement and it would help. It wasn't going to replace brokers. This, to me, seems evidence of that. It's not replacing brokers, it's helping them.

[03:28] Dalia Barsoum: One hundred percent. This is making us more powerful brokers. It's like having an assistant that saves you time, makes you stronger, faster, smarter, to free up your time to focus on what you came to this industry to do, which is serving more people and getting your time back to have a fulfilling business that can support you and your family the way you envisioned.

[03:53] AI still needs human judgment. You cannot have AI run the show for you. What's effective is to have it do certain things within boundaries, but oversee it, train it, and that's where the human touch comes in. Then you can focus on what you're really good at that machines cannot replace.

[04:13] Fergal McAlinden: Absolutely. Let's talk a little bit about the current market. We all know that there are challenges for a lot of borrowers, challenges for a lot of clients. What type of market have you been seeing this year and is it different to what we saw in 2025?

[04:25] Dalia Barsoum: So, we're still seeing pain in this market. Let me put it this way. Obviously when the rates went up, things started to shift and it's been a couple of years now. We're still seeing pain with debt levels, with values.

[04:44] Having said that, and I tell everybody, in every obstacle there is an opportunity. If we know what problems to solve for in this environment and there are people who need our help, then we're going to be able to reach out to new types of clients and solve new problems. We're starting to do that in our brokerage and it did open up doors for us because I think sometimes we get comfortable doing the same thing over and over and over.

[05:11] I'm still seeing pain. I recently published a book actually called The Rebound Advantage that talks about financial setbacks, just because we're still seeing quite a bit of that. That's an opportunity for brokers to help clients who are in different pain situations.

[05:28] But also, here's the thing. I find that the media brushes everything with the same brush and obviously tries to magnify the negative. I can tell you that in this market there are clients that are growing without pain and investing and they're still doing well. So the question for us brokers: how can we reach the growing trends in this economy and serve them and solve a problem?

[05:53] Fergal McAlinden: I think maybe at CMP we're a little bit more attuned to it because we cover the mortgage and real estate sectors more than others maybe. But what we always hear is that the housing market downturn has regional differences. Maybe some parts of the country aren't doing well but others are flourishing.

[06:09] Dalia Barsoum: Of course. Yes. I'm talking Ontario primarily.

[06:11] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. But even within Ontario, there are certain pockets that are doing very well. Certain types of property, even within the condo sector. So-called dog crates aren't doing well, but others are actually flourishing. It's a nuanced picture, I think.

[06:25] Dalia Barsoum: One hundred percent. On that note, for example, I'm seeing clients that are doing well in cottage country, believe it or not, but mass market in some pockets is not doing well. So again, you have to deconstruct and look for pockets of growth and opportunity. Even in an environment like this, you will find them. If you solve the problem, that's how you grow your volume and continue to progress, even though the big picture, when you zoom out, seems to be dark and ugly.

[06:59] Fergal McAlinden: No, that's the right attitude for sure. Looking forward to seeing what's next from Wisely AI. Anything that you're focusing on for the next few months or any trends you have your eye on?

[07:07] Dalia Barsoum: So just the focus is, again, The Rebound Advantage, the book that I put out. It's not just for clients. It's for me to share with everybody in the industry that has experienced a financial setback in their business, but also as a tool to help their clients.

[07:22] I am looking forward to sharing more of that. And then on the Wisely AI front, just putting an AI compliance support minion in the hands of those who need it. We're bringing more minions to the table in 2027 on other fronts of the mortgage journey. So that's the focus.

[07:37] Fergal McAlinden: Perfect. Well, I always appreciate your time. Pleasure to talk to you. Best of luck.

[07:41] Dalia Barsoum: Thank you very much. Thank you.

items.title: Insider: Ontario And Quebec Are Running Opposite Housing Experiments
items.description:
I have lost count of how many times I have heard that Toronto and Vancouver are a special case. Too expensive, too much debt, a local hangover. October is getting in the way of that story.

In CREA's residential numbers, Greater Toronto sales were down 7.9% from last October. Greater Vancouver was down 10.7%. Calgary was down 12.8%. Ottawa was down 10.8%. Montreal was down 17.6%. The country was down 10.6%. If those two cities were still a quarantine zone, the others would not be on that list.

Prices have not followed in every market, and that is the part worth sitting with. Calgary's benchmark was unchanged at $569,300. Montreal's was still up 1.4%, to $591,400. Ottawa was only down 1.5%. Toronto is down 4.4% on the year and 13.7% over three years. Vancouver is down 5.2%. Volume goes first. Price lags. Then the "isolated incident" starts to look like a leading indicator.

Two provinces, opposite directions

That national demand story sits on top of a supply split I still think is the more interesting chart in this release. Ontario recorded 33,510 new residential listings in October, 8.8% fewer than a year ago, against 14,053 sales, down 8.7%. Quebec went the other way on supply: 13,864 new listings, up 6.2%, against 7,451 sales, down 12.6%. Ontario's new listings have run below year-ago levels for essentially all of 2026. Quebec's have run above.

Chart: New listings, year-over-year %, Ontario vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

The Greater Toronto benchmark is $928,800, down 4.4% year over year. Mississauga is down 8.5%. Quebec CMA is up 5.1%, and 33.6% over three years. Ontario is tightening the shelf and still losing price. Quebec is adding listings and still gaining some.

Toronto tightened by subtraction

Through the first ten months of 2026, the Greater Toronto Area logged 145,345 new listings, 14.7% fewer than the same period last year. Sales were 52,694, down only 1.8%. The year-to-date sales-to-new-listings ratio rose to 36.3% from 31.5%.

That "improvement" came from sellers stepping back. Buyers did not arrive. Even after a year of withdrawals, Toronto's seasonally adjusted ratio was 39.1% in October, still under the 45% floor of CREA's balanced range.

Chart: Sales-to-new-listings ratio, seasonally adjusted. Toronto vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

Montreal moved the other way. Year-to-date new listings rose 6.3% to 69,458 while sales fell 8.7% to 37,091, pulling the ratio down to 53.4% from 62.2%. Montreal is loosening from a seller's market toward balance. Toronto is crawling up from a buyer's market by shrinking the choice set.

Chart: Months of inventory, seasonally adjusted. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

I would not tell a Quebec builder the Ontario correction has landed in Montreal prices. I also would not tell them demand is insulated. Montreal sales were down 17.6% in October, in a market where prices are still rising. Some of that is rates. Montreal's benchmark sits about $337,000 below Toronto's, so a hike bites less than it does on a GTA loan. Some of it, in my view, is confidence and equity travelling. When Toronto and Vancouver values fall, owners feel poorer. They spend less and they move less. Investors who hold product in more than one city get careful. Lenders do too. I cannot show you a contagion index. I can show you volumes weakening in places that were supposed to be fine.

The pipeline tells the longer story

Resale listings are this month's supply. Housing starts are the supply of 2029 and 2030.

From January through September 2026, Ontario's housing starts averaged a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 61,200, according to CMHC data compiled on Homies stats. Quebec averaged about 60,100. Ontario's pace is down 5.7% from the same months of 2025. Quebec's is up 1.8%.

Those two numbers are nearly identical. The provinces are not. Statistics Canada estimates Ontario's population at about 16.26 million and Quebec's at about 9.07 million as of July 2026. Per 1,000 residents, Quebec is starting homes at an annualized pace of roughly 6.6. Ontario is at roughly 3.8.

Chart: Housing starts, seasonally adjusted annual rate, Ontario vs Quebec, indexed to January 2022. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CMHC via Statistics Canada.

Ontario's resale market is reaching balance by holding product back. Its development pipeline is doing the same thing. If the demand softness in Toronto is a leading indicator rather than a local mess, that is a problem for anyone underwriting 2028 absorption in the rest of the country.

The condo collapse is a resale problem first

Nationally, condo starts from January through September totalled 25,719, down 34.8% from 39,446 in the same months of 2025. Purpose-built rental starts rose 8.6% to 90,623.

Chart: Condo vs rental housing starts, Canada, indexed to January 2023. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CMHC via Statistics Canada.

Presale condo projects need buyers willing to pay tomorrow's price today, and lenders need those presales before construction financing flows. When the GTA resale benchmark is down 13.7% over three years, the comparable undercuts the presale, the presales do not get sold, and the project does not start.

A rate hike makes that worse. The Bank of Canada raised the overnight rate to 2.50% from 2.25% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023. Then the five-year Canada bond, the thing lenders actually price a fixed mortgage off, jumped from 3.33% to 3.60% in under a week, as Robert McLister noted in the Financial Post on November 16. Buying power got tighter after the October deals were already written.

Confidence was not exactly roaring into that. The Bloomberg-Nanos Canadian Confidence Index was 50.98 for the four weeks ending October 30, below its long-term average of 54.65. The expectations index, which includes the outlook for the economy and property prices, sat at 47.77. Nik Nanos called it the slow lane. A presale buyer is being asked to commit years out, with their home equity worth less and their fixed rate already moving. Rental is holding up because its financing does not depend on those retail buyers in the same way. That is a real offset. It does not replace the ownership units a turned cycle will need.

Chart: Active residential listings, Ontario vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

What it means

For builders: Quebec still has rising benchmarks and a ratio in balanced territory, which is the kind of comparable set that can support a presale. Ontario does not, and October's rate move does not help. I would not plan a national absorption number as if the demand problem stopped at the GTA border.

For policymakers: Ontario's resale "balance" is not proof the supply problem is solved. Sellers stopped listing. Builders stopped starting. Both are rational. Together they set up the next shortage. National inventory is about 197,000 listings, a little above CREA's long-term average of 190,000, with five months of supply. On paper, Canada looks balanced. Underneath, the biggest province is balancing by doing less, and the sales weakness that started in Toronto and Vancouver is no longer staying there. If we "solve" a glut by starting fewer homes, what does 2029 look like? The monthly CREA release will not answer that. The starts number might.

items.title: Firm Capital Buys Highlight Of Mississauga Project Under Creditor Protection For $74.3M
items.description:
A large condo project in Mississauga that became insolvent and was placed under creditor protection mid-construction over four years ago has officially been sold, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court.

The project is known as Highlight of Mississauga and is located at 4064, 4070, and 4078 Dixie Road, right across the street from Rockwood Mall in Mississauga.

The developer was a company called Hazelton Development Corporation (HDC) and the project website identifies an individual named Du Zhixian as the company’s President. Court documents also refer to him as Joe Du, and note that the company is majority-owned by “a prominent construction family in China.”

For the site, Hazelton Development Corporation was developing a 14-storey project with 265 strata units, including both condos and townhomes. Presales launched around May 2018 and 261 of 265 units were pre-sold, generating a total of $111,633,085 in revenue.

Construction commenced in September 2019 and completion was targeted for April 2021, but the project faced delays and liquidity issues that resulted in HDC seeking out creditor protection under the federal Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA) in April 2022, by which construction had reached Level 12.

The Debts

For the project, Hazelton took out a first-ranking mortgage with Meridian Credit Union in May 2019 for a construction loan with a principal amount of up to $50 million, plus a stand-by letter of credit facility up to $2 million.

It also took out a second mortgage with Centurion Mortgage Capital Corporation — which was folded into Centurion Asset Management in 2024 — for a construction facility of up to $19.9 million, plus a cost-overrun facility up to $3.5 million.

As of the time of their filing, HDC owed approximately $20,694,142 to Meridian and $20,673,626 to Centurion, for a total of $41,367,768, with interest continuing to accrue.

According to HDC, certain shareholders also loaned HDC approximately $6.35 million between September 2019 and March 2022, and a company called Triumph Eastern Investments Inc. also advanced six loans between October 2021 and March 2022.

Various amounts were also owed to contractors.

The Insolvency

Hazelton Development Corporation said they faced trouble from the onset as the COVID-19 pandemic hit just a few months after construction commenced. In March 2020, they notified purchasers that the project would be delayed. Construction later resumed, but HDC had to issue additional delay notices in May 2021, November 2021, January 2022, and March 2022.

“The initial construction budget for the Project was $101,183,823,” said HDC. “By November 2021, under previous management, the forecasted construction budget had increased by $11,672,011 to $113,669,237. These increases were due to, among other things: two significant delays on account of Covid-19 lock-downs, an increased level of supervision and project management, substantial increases to the hard costs budget for concrete, masonry, mechanical equipment and electrical work, and various material increases to the soft costs budget.”

Construction loan agreements often include obligations that borrowers maintain a minimum debt-to-equity ratio, but although HDC was able to raise additional equity from shareholders, it was not enough to satisfy Meridian’s requirement, and the lender ceased advances in July 2021, forcing HDC to rely on Centurion and buyer deposits.

In March 2022, the Du family bought out a group of shareholders, which gave them an 80% stake in HDC, and brought in new management to stabilize the project. A month later, in April 2022, HDC filed for creditor protection.

The Highlight of Mississauga as of March 2026. (Grant Thornton)

Under Creditor Protection

In July 2022, Toronto-based non-bank lender Firm Capital (TSX: FC) emerged as a sponsor and agreed to loan up to $80 million to pay off various debts and finance the construction of Highlight of Mississauga. The plan was approved, and construction then resumed.

In February 2023, the court then granted an order allowing the presale purchasers to be given two options. The first option would allow them to carry on with the purchase under revised terms, while the second option would terminate the presale agreement and see the buyer be compensated for their deposit with a 12% premium.

Although there were disputes with contractors and various other delays, construction continued and reached approximately 92.6% completion by February 2026, when the court-appointed Monitor said that “The ongoing deficiencies, construction challenges, weather-related delays, rising completion costs, and the Company’s funding constraints, have resulted in further delays to completion” and that “The Monitor understands that completion of the Project may no longer be feasible.”

By then, most of the presale purchasers had taken the compensation option and there were 197 unsold units. Lien claims by contractors had also continued to pile up, totalling to $10,802,325.

The Sale

The court-ordered sales process commenced in late-February. According to a report prepared by the Monitor, 15 parties signed confidentiality agreements and five toured the site. One party submitted a letter of intent in June, but reduced their offer during negotiations the following month, citing higher-than-anticipated expected taxes.

The Monitor then engaged other bidders, but could not find a better offer. Feedback from the market was that the project was better suited as a rental building, that the cost to complete was anywhere from $15 million to $30 million, and that the required remedial work was an added level of uncertainty.

“When it became apparent that there would be no unconditional bids,” said the Monitor, Firm Capital then began discussions to buy the project themselves through a reverse vesting order that would see them buy the shares of Hazelton Development Corporation — a share sale — instead of directly buying the real estate. Firm Capital’s purchase agreement also required that the remaining 48 presale contracts be terminated.

The purchase price is equivalent to the sum of various floating amounts, totalling to around $73.5 million, plus $802,000 in cash consideration, for a total of around $74.3 million estimated at September 30, 2026.

The sale approval court hearing was originally scheduled for October 1, but was then delayed due to various stakeholders raising objections. The hearing was delayed to October 22, then October 26, before it was finally approved by the Ontario Superior Court on November 4.

items._ogDesc: Canadian inflation held at 3.1% in October, while property taxes rose 3.8%, outpacing overall price growth as Ontario tax arrears climbed.
items.body:
Canada’s headline inflation remains elevated, but at least it didn’t get worse. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows annual headline CPI growth held at 3.1% in October. The lack of acceleration would be good news if not for broadening inflation. Core measures didn’t clarify much this month, but one thing was clear—property taxes are still ripping while arrears climb.

Canadian Inflation Holds At 3.1%, Tamed By Cooling Gas Prices

Annual CPI growth rate.

Annual growth of CPI held at 3.1% in October, remaining elevated but unchanged from September. Helping to tame growth was a deceleration in gasoline prices, which fell 2.5% in the month but were up 30.9% from last year. The agency also notes that annual declines for cellphone plans (-6.2%) helped, though prices may not be lower. Cell phone plans have been a persistent downward pressure due to methodology, not because people are paying less.

Hard Core? Canada’s “Stable” Core CPI Measures Moved Lower, Higher, and Stalled

Canada’s Core CPI measures are designed to provide some clarity, and minimize headline volatility. Unfortunately, Canada’s three big core measures all told a different story last month.

CPI median’s annual growth was unchanged at 2.0%. The core measure tracks the midpoint of price changes, weighted by spending.

CPI-trim slowed from 1.9% to 1.8% in October. This measure excludes the largest upward and downward movements, ideally eliminating the volatility. In practice, prices take the elevator up and the stairs down. As a result, much larger price surges can be neutralized by much smaller declines.

CPI-common accelerated to 2.5% y/y in October, up from 2.4% in September. This measure tracks price movements across categories, filtering out fluctuations for individual items.

No measure is perfect, and the mixed direction reveals how flawed the shift to annual re-indexing has been. The agency’s Census intervals are spaced out to minimize the volatility of resource allocation. However, StatCan argues the pricing of those resources needs to be re-indexed annually.

Canadian Property Tax Growth Slows, But Still Faster Than Inflation

Annual growth of property taxes and special charges.

Every October StatCan’s CPI reports property taxes and other special charges. The segment saw prices rise 3.8% from last year, down from 5.6% reported in 2025. Slower than recent years, but it’s coming down from the sharpest surge since the early ’90s. At the same time, it’s nearly double the BoC’s target rate of inflation, and well above its upper bound of tolerance.

Slower-but-still-elevated property tax and special charges are also unlikely to feel like relief. The 3.3% annual growth in Ontario follows last year’s 5.5% jump. It’s been accompanied by a sharp rise in property tax arrears. Recent filings in the region reveal a property tax arrears rate of up to 11.9% in its largest municipalities.

items.title: Bank Of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem Stepping Down
items.description:
Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem is stepping down next June.

The Bank’s Board of Directors announced Monday that Macklem has told them he won’t seek a second term when his seven-year term ends on June 2, 2027.

The Board has started a search for the next Governor.

“It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada,” Macklem said. “My time as Governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world. The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate.”

Macklem thanked the Board, the Minister of Finance, and the Prime Minister for entrusting him with the stewardship of Canada’s central bank.

“It is a privilege to serve as Governor, and I remain fully committed to fulfilling my responsibilities and delivering for Canadians through the remainder of my term,” he said.

The independent directors on the Board have formed a Search Committee to run the recruitment process. Executive recruiting firm Egon Zehnder is helping them, and the Bank is inviting interested candidates to read the Executive Brief for the role and contact Egon Zehnder confidentially.

The Bank expects to finish the search by spring 2027.

Subject to approval from the Minister of Finance and federal Cabinet, the Board’s independent directors will appoint the next Governor to a seven-year term starting June 3, 2027.

Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian Immigration Changes To Double Population Growth Rate: BMO

Canada’s looking to boost its immigration, but it hasn’t framed it that way. Officially, the target is to add 380,000 new permanent residents per year for 2027-29. However, BMO economists estimate that special measures push the total to 660,000 for 2027. The massive change has the bank nearly doubling its population growth forecast. Though it’s worth distinguishing between a target and reality. Canada’s foreign student tapering only began after applications dropped sharply, suggesting exhausted demand.

Canadian Housing Affordability’s Record Recovery May End Soon: NBF

Housing affordability across Canada has made a record 11 straight quarters of improvement. That sounds impressive, but the details are less flattering. Mortgage payments on a typical home would consume 50.9% of a median household’s income at this level. Even with the record length of improvements, this is still one of the worst markets for buyers in history. National Bank economists warn this may also be as good as it gets in the near-term, as mortgage rates are set to climb.

Canada To Add 200,000 Permanent Resident Spots, Housing Boost Limited

Canada’s immigration plan will boost permanent residents 50% higher than the headline data suggests. It’s seen as a boost to the economy, especially housing demand, but that may not be the case. The added capacity targets those already in the country and looking to stay. While this can mean less churn and ultimately more people, demand doesn’t get a direct boost. Their consumption is already reflected in the current data.

Ontario Real Estate

Ontario Property Tax Arrears Hit 24-Year High, Brampton Leads At 11.9%

Ontario property tax arrears are at a 24-year high, driven by Toronto’s suburbs. Filings show the property tax arrears rate hit 7.2% of the $34.1 billion in levies for 2025, up 2.46 points since 2019. The rate is now at its highest level since 2001, but there’s an important distinction here. Today, the rate is climbing, but back then it was falling after the early ‘90s real estate bubble popped. Coincidentally, property taxes just made their biggest increase since the early ’90s.

Toronto Real Estate

Over 1 In 8 Greater Toronto Rental Units Sit Vacant As Completions Hit A Record

Greater Toronto’s rental construction boom means a lot of supply is sitting empty. The often-reported vacancy rate for stabilized purpose-built rentals fell from 5.4% to 3.0% in Q3. The catch is stabilized, which excludes buildings that have never hit 95% occupancy. In a normal market, it may not be a big difference; including all purpose-built units means a 13.3% vacancy rate. Even with 1 in 8 units vacant, there are 34,545 more currently under construction, nearly half of the units being built across Canada. So far, there’s been minimal progress on prices, but that can change fast with a record supply glut on the way.

items.body:
The Ontario real estate correction has another ominous point—unpaid property taxes. Filings with the Government of Ontario show municipalities are still struggling to collect $2.43 billion in overdue property taxes at the end of 2025. The filings show the arrears rate of property taxes is now at the highest level since 2001.

About Today’s Data

Today, we’re looking at the 2025 property tax arrears rate for Ontario municipalities. This is the share of each year’s levy that was still unpaid at year’s end, according to each municipality’s filings. For the provincial rate, we’re using the 316 out of 414 municipalities that filed in 2025, and 392 that are up to date for 2024. While this covers the lion’s share of dollar value, Hamilton’s filings are notably unavailable. The city’s 2024 filing was also unavailable, so it appears someone is behind on their homework.

Ontario Property Tax Arrears Hit Highest Level Since 2001

Ontario property taxes in arrears: Delinquent property taxes as a share of total property tax levies, 2000 to 2025.

Source: Government of Ontario; Better Dwelling.

Ontario’s arrears rate hit 7.2% of 2025 property taxes, representing $2.4 billion of the $34.1 billion in levies. The rate is a sharp jump of 48 basis points (bps) from 2024 and 246 bps since 2019. It’s the highest arrears rate for the province since 2001, making it a generational high. A key difference here is that the rate was falling back then, whereas today it’s rising—and where it stops is anyone’s guess.

Ontario’s Major Cities See Property Tax Arrears Hit Up To 11.9%

Property taxes in arrears: Delinquent property taxes as a share of total property tax levies, 2025. Largest municipalities with up-to-date filings.

Source: Ontario municipality filings; Better Dwelling.

Out of Ontario’s largest cities with filings, Brampton’s 11.9% arrears rate is by far the highest in the province. It’s followed by Vaughan at 9.9%, and Kitchener at 8.9%. All three cities have been above average in recent years, and they’re unusually high.

Brampton’s rate is its highest since 2004, while Vaughan and Kitchener are at their highest since 2001. Brampton also went from below average in 2021 to the highest of the large cities in just four years.

In contrast, Toronto’s 2025 property tax arrears rate of 6.6% is somewhat outperforming. The City represents over 1 in 5 dollars of 2025 property taxes in arrears, but levies nearly a quarter of the province’s property tax. In the provincial context, it’s better than average. However, benchmarked against itself, this is the city’s highest rate since 2001. Once again, the difference here is that the rate was falling back then after property taxes in arrears quadrupled from 1988 to 1993 over the six cities that are now Toronto.

It’s probably not a coincidence that property taxes and special levies just made their largest jump since the early ’90s, either. Everyone loves a fast-growing city when the market is booming, but not so much once it’s time to pay those bills.

items.title: Supreme Court of Canada dismisses bid to appeal B.C. foreign buyer tax case
items.description:
The Supreme Court of Canada won't hear an appeal challenging the application of British Columbia's foreign buyer tax on a real estate purchase involving joint ownership by a Canadian citizen and a foreign national. 
 The B.C.
items._ogDesc: The Supreme Court of Canada won't hear an appeal challenging the application of British Columbia's foreign buyer tax on a real estate purchase involving joint ownership by a Canadian citizen and a foreign national. The B.C.
items.body:
The Supreme Court of Canada won't hear an appeal challenging the application of British Columbia's foreign buyer tax on a real estate purchase involving joint ownership by a Canadian citizen and a foreign national.

The B.C. Court of Appeal had previously dismissed an appeal brought by a couple who jointly bought an apartment in Richmond, B.C., putting 95 per cent in the Canadian woman's name, and five per cent in the name of her foreign partner.

But the man had actually paid 40 per cent of the purchase price, with the woman explaining the disparity by saying it was a Chinese custom for a husband to pay a "bride price" by buying his wife a home.

The couple, who were engaged in 2014 when they bought the home under a presale contract, paid the foreign buyer tax on only the five per cent registered to the foreign man, but an audit later found the tax "payable on the fair market value of the whole property."

The B.C. government had told the lower court the rule was meant to "prevent tax avoidance by foreign investors who own beneficial interests held indirectly by others."

The Supreme Court of Canada refused the couple leave to appeal on Thursday.

The couple had claimed imposing the tax on the entire value of the property was "profoundly unfair," but the three-judge panel of the Appeal Court found they could have avoided paying the tax on the property's entire value if they had registered ownership based on their contributions to the purchase price.

The appellate ruling from earlier this year said the man, Li-Yuan Chuang, paid 40 per cent of the purchase price, but registered only a five per cent stake in the property, which the couple declared to have a value of $474,500 at the time of purchase.

His Canadian partner, Chia-Wen Hsia, said it was "customary in Chinese culture to pay for ‘bride price’ as in the husband buying a house for the wife."

"In my husband’s case, he is not rich so he could only pay for part of the purchase price,” Hsia is quoted as saying in the appellate ruling.

The B.C. Supreme Court initially dismissed the couple's legal challenge in 2024.

The most recent assessed value for the two-bedroom apartment in the Avanti Richmond complex is $820,000.

The original B.C. Supreme Court ruling said a B.C. Finance Ministry tax analyst put the additional tax owed by the couple at just over $126,000.

The B.C. foreign buyer tax is 20 per cent of market value.

The couple's lawyer, Massao Morinaga, said they had no comment about the Supreme Court of Canada's dismissal of the case.

He said it was the "end of the road judicially," but the current foreign buyer tax legislation is drafted in a way that "captures situations that are inequitable."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press
